subtopic: HUNGARY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: HUNGARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday I said that a note of protest would be sent to the Hungarian government expressing the strong disapproval of the Canadian government and the Canadian people of the execution of former Premier Nagy of Hungary and his associates. I now wish to inform the house that today a note was delivered to the Hungarian representative at the United Nations, the material portions of which are as follows:
The revulsion and shock manifest throughout the world at the news of the execution of Imre Nagy, former premier of Hungary and his associates, is shared by the government and the people of Canada. The fact that the victims were taken into custody after assurances were given by the Hungarian government that no sanctions would be taken against them and that they could proceed freely to their homes makes their execution the more reprehensible.
It is greatly to be regretted that the Hungarian government has seen fit to carry out these harsh reprisals which flout the principles of justice and worsen the international climate. In 1956 and in 1957 world opinion expressed itself unmistakably on the tragic events in Hungary through debates in the United Nations and in the report of the special United Nations committee of investigation. These executions are therefore considered by the Canadian government as part of an unjustifiable terrorist policy which is abhorrent to the people of Canada and which makes it difficult to maintain the hope that the Hungarian government, along with other governments of eastern Europe, will be able to move forward towards a more liberal dispensation for their peoples.

speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister, based upon a communication I have received from local 4527, United Mine Workers of America, and upon press reports indicating further cutbacks and mine closures in Nova Scotia. speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in so far as the situation in Nova Scotia is concerned, there has been such an overproduction of coal that it has required action on the part of the coal producing companies. The suggestion was made that the federal government might place itself in the position of a guarantor in respect of certain advances to be made to the coal companies, thereby providing a continuance of production until such time as the accumulation of more than 1 million tons of coal has been sold.
This represents the situation at the present time, but consideration has been given to the representations which have been made. As yet, however, I am not in a position to say whether it would be appropriate from a constitutional point of view for the national government to take the action suggested. In addition, the whole situation is being canvassed with a view to ameliorating to the greatest possible degree the discomfort caused to the workers and their families through the temporary discontinuance of production.

The Canada Shipping Act was amended in 1956 to deal with the oil pollution problem, and the oil pollution prevention regulations were made pursuant to the new provisions of the act. These regulations forbid the dumping of fuel oil from ships' tanks into the domestic waters of Canada. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam took exception to the stand taken by the Minister of Finance with regard to his request that all sections of the Canadian economy try to hold the price and wage line, and that increases should be based upon increased productivity. As the hon. member must have known, because it is detailed in the budget speech, the minister expects a drop in revenue of $387 million, of which more than half or some $200 million is due to tax reductions made by this government, but almost all the remainder is due to a falling off in corporation profits.
Today I received a bulletin which gave the results of a survey of 1,069 manufacturing companies employing more than 441,000 people in 1957. It shows that profits dropped from 5.8 cents on each dollar of sales in 1956 to 5.2 cents last year, that is 1957. Of this 1957 profit, 2.3 cents went to shareholders and 2.9 cents were plowed back into the business with, of course, a resulting increase in employment opportunities. Over the last ten years, according to this survey which has been made, the average profits have been 5.72 cents on each dollar of sales, so the profits in 1957 were 10 per cent below the ten-year average.
Mr. Speaker, this government has turned this nation into a world trading nation, as compared with the inclinations of the previous government to limit us to a hemispheric trading nation. For instance, in 1957 we had the highest exports on record in Canadian history, and these include the highest exports ever known to the United States. This year, in the first five months the total exports achieved an even greater height than in 1957. In fact this year our total exports for the

first five months are $1,952.9 million as compared with $1,936.4 million in the first five months last year. This year United Kingdom and commonwealth figures are up from $378 million to $420 million and the United States figure is slightly down, by 1.8 per cent. But imports from the United States are down by $300 million and imports from the United Kingdom are up by $5 million. The effect of this will be corrective to a limited degree on our balance of payments deficit, which amounted to $1.4 billion last year.
The minister has pointed out that the chronic nature of our massive trade imbalance with the United States requires energetic corrective measures. These huge trade deficits, accompanied as they are by heavy increases in our long-term indebtedness to the United States, carry serious implications for the future health and economic independence of our country. The heavy concentration of our foreign trade on the United States means that the Canadian economy is extremely vulnerable to the United States economic and political climate, and to shifts in its trading policy.
I believe the minister pointed out that the proposed European free trade area represents a market which is equivalent in population to the United States. In that regard we must do our best to maintain our trade position with that area as it comes into being. I believe the government is doing a job which will have lasting and beneficial effects on our Canadian economy, as we will be less subject to the sudden fluctuations in the United States, although they will always remain our best customer, the customer who buys most of our goods and from whom we buy most of our goods.
We will, however, develop a very large trade with the rest of the world which will act as a balance wheel for this rather overwhelming north-south trade pattern as it exists today.
The Budget-Mr. Broome
I would like to say a few words with respect to the increases in pensions brought forward by the government, and also with respect to the indication that the civil service pensions are to be reviewed. It has been mentioned that some time during this parliamentary session some such measures will be introduced to this house. The condition of the superannuated civil servant who retired in 1948, or any time prior to that year, is rather unenviable, because the previous government did not keep the wage scale of the civil servants anywhere in line with that of industry. For instance, in 1946 a letter carrier received a salary of $150 a month whereas in 1957, ten years later, he received $300 a month. In 1948 a clerk grade 2 in the customs department received $1,860 a year, whereas in 1958 he will receive $3,150 a year. Because pensions are tied to earnings, the resulting pensions are proportionately low for those earlier years. With the consent of the house I would now like to place on record a table which I have prepared indicating the differences between 1946 and 1958.

In regard to our trade pattern, the fact that our population increase was the highest on record, partly as a result of natural increase and partly as a result of the heavy immigration program, has tended to make our unemployment problems more acute, but at the same time is building up the domestic market which will in turn have a levelling and balancing effect on our internal economy. Because of our rapidly increasing population we should endeavour to have more manufacturing done in Canada. In 1957 the total production of passenger cars in this country was 340,016, while in 1937 the figure was 153,046.
In the 1930's the tariff schedule allowed the importation of parts from the United States on the basis that if total car production was 10,000 units or less and had a commonwealth content of 40 per cent, then the imported parts would be duty free. If it was 20,000 units or less the commonwealth content would have to be 50 per cent, and if it was over 20,000 units then the commonwealth content would have to be 60 per cent.
I would suggest that a review of the importation of parts used in automobile manufacture might very well show that there is room for a greatly expanded operation by the automobile companies on this side of the border, if they so desire, with a consequent increase in employment opportunities in this country. It may be that the content requirement might be increased, at least by some percentage; but in any event I feel some study of this question should be undertaken to see just what is involved and what can be done to increase manufacturing in Canada.
The hon. member for Essex East has bitterly complained time after time about the importation of United Kingdom cars and the fact that opportunities for employment in this country have been thereby decreased. I have checked into this matter, and I find that the importation of complete passenger and truck units during last year from the United States totalled about $75 million and the importation of European cars totalled around $54 million. There was a total of

15,298 passenger car units worth $46 million imported from the United States.
The sum and substance of this is that as we increase manufacturing in Canada we promote jobs; and because of the control of our manufacturing set-up-54 per cent of control being outside of Canada, mainly within the United States-there is a tendency on the part of the companies to concentrate their manufacturing operations in their parent plants, leaving the Canadian companies as assembly operations and distribution and sales organizations. This tendency to treat the Canadian company as a branch plant takes away from it the opportunity to develop foreign trade. It also minimizes the possibilities of expansion within this country. In other words, it is being operated in many cases for the benefit of the parent company, not only with respect to sales and how they should be carried on but also with respect to employment opportunities.
I am rather familiar with the field of engineering, and have been most distressed to find that wherever one goes one finds that many Canadian companies, besides a great number of the foreign-owned subsidiary companies and also some municipalities, seem to feel that Canadian engineers and architects do not have what they require and that they must go to the United States to secure these services. I believe that in all government contracts a clause should be inserted to the effect that such services shall be supplied from within Canada. We should take the lead, thereby influencing our junior levels of government to follow along the same lines.
I have in my hand a clipping from the Toronto Telegram of April 15, 1958, in which it is stated that individual engineers, who insist on remaining unnamed, are being replaced by United States engineers. It also mentions that the contract for the improvement of the city approaches to the skyway just outside Hamilton was let to engineers from outside the country. There are undoubtedly many engineering problems which require specialized skills not available in Canada, but in general the Canadian engineering and architectural professions can take care of the great bulk of our requirements.

I could not close without making at least one or two references to the benefits which I believe will ensue from the appointment of the Borden commission on energy. I attended several of the hearings in western Canada, and I can assure the house that the commission is doing a tremendous job. This is a job which needed to be done and will, I am sure, result in a much healthier atmosphere in the oil and gas industries. The problems of commercial preference, of markets in the northwest, of the Montreal market, are all being investigated to the end that there should be greater markets for Canadian oil and a greater utilization of petroleum resources through manufacturing carried on in our country.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the Minister of Finance has done a job which was incomparably more difficult than that which faced any of his predecessors, and that he deserves the thanks of this nation for having brought forth a budget which I feel is so clearly tailored to meet the needs of this country.

Mr. Speaker, the budget is the instrument by which the commitments made by the party forming the government are translated into concrete form. Envisaged in this aspect, never has a budget sounded more paradoxical than that presented by the Minister of Finance on June 17. Indeed, we all have vividly in our minds those broad and glowing commitments which were made by the present government during the recent political campaign.
Here are a few of those commitments: the lowering of the general level of taxation; a special public works program; increased assistance to municipalities; guaranteed prices to fishermen for their fish; full employment to all; reduction of the gross national debt; a balanced budget and the stimulating of trade.
Just how many of these commitments are to be implemented following the forecast made in the context of the budget now before this house? Very few and scanty budgetary items are there toward the fulfilment of those countless promises. To the average wage earner of the country, to the Canadian taxpayer, to the industrialist and the businessman, to the farmer, the fisherman, the miner, to the hundreds of thousands of unemployed, visions of yesterday have become the delusions of today; dreams of the past have dissipated, to make room for anxiety and concern in the future.
Mr. Speaker, it has been said that too much time has been taken by the individual members of this house to speak of the needs of their respective constituencies. Little
The Budget-Mr. Michaud wonder, in the light of the economic conditions prevailing in every section of the country, that individual members feel it their duty to voice to the responsible legislative body of the country, that is the government, the wants of their constituents. As the representative in this house of the people of Kent county, I feel I would be remiss in my duty if I failed to tell this government of the uncertainty, in some cases of the distress, of my constituents at the present time.
While the government lays great claim to its so-called huge public works program to create employment, I respectfully submit that the sources of employment in my own province of New Brunswick have drastically declined as compared with immediate past years. Hundreds of workers who secured employment at Camp Gagetown during the last four or five years are idle, unable to secure further work on that project. Hundreds of workers who in the past were employed on government projects at Labrador are tediously waiting for recalls which are not forthcoming. Hundreds of woodsmen who found gainful employment in the flourishing pulp and lumber industry in the immediate past stand idle in the face of this sudden stagnation in that industry.
While the Minister of Public Works loudly proclaims that thousands and thousands of people have been put to work under a special works program, the number of unemployed workers in our province remains at unusual heights. I ask the government to give immediate attention to this crucial situation before a full-scale depression such as we have already had in this country again fully develops.
I do not hesitate to state what has already been stated often in this house; that if it were not for the various social measures brought in by the preceding Liberal administration, such as old age pensions, family allowances, unemployment insurance and so on, we would now be living in economic conditions as depressed as those of the early thirties. It is all very well for the government to maintain its attitude of self-contentment when these critical situations are called to its attention. The people are no longer content with this display of inertia and indifference on the part of the government, and with its failure to act as promised to remedy this depressed state of affairs.
Surely there are projects to be initiated in the maritime provinces which could provide employment at the present time. I indicated one which, I submit, is of major importance, in the course of my speech during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, namely the

The Budget-Mr. Michaud Chignecto canal. If this project was important enough to warrant the Prime Minister's attention during election time, surely it should warrant that same attention as a means of relieving unemployment. There are many other useful projects of a similar nature, and with the same usefulness of purpose, that should command the attention of this government in the present circumstances. What our working class expects is nothing less than what it has a right to expect and what was solemnly promised to it by this government-work which will permit them to sustain themselves and their families. I urge the government to act now.
I should like to take advantage of this budget debate to deal specifically with one of the most important sectors of our economy, agriculture. During the last two election campaigns our farmers have been led to believe by the Conservative spokesmen, and particularly by the Prime Minister, that they can expect a completely new deal from the present government and a solution to all their many problems. It is still too early to judge the record of the present government in this regard, but I want to say to the hon. ministers opposite that we will be watching their activities very closely and will do our utmost to see that they live up to their election promises. In addition, anything we can do to force the hand of the government in this matter we shall certainly do.
Representatives of all parties agree that the situation in which the Canadian farmer finds himself today is not satisfactory. In many parts of the country our farm economy has not kept pace with the progress and development of some other aspects of our economy. Many of the problems with which farmers are faced today are extremely complicated; and some of them, such as the marketing of surplus products, have international complications.
In the area which I represent, the problem which concerns us most is the preservation of the family farm. The family farm is the very basis of our society in New Brunswick, and indeed in most parts of Canada. But today the family farm is in danger of being wiped out in the face of competition from large scale industrial methods applied to agriculture. Let me give you but one example. In many parts of Canada today, broiler chickens are being produced in vast numbers by commercial organizations under conditions and in quantities with which our farmers cannot compete. There is a tendency on behalf of these large commercial companies to get

control of all phases of agricultural production and marketing. This is a real danger for our farmers, and that is why I feel everything possible must be done to assist the family farm to survive.
All those who are sincerely interested in the welfare of the Canadian farmer are aware of the many steps taken by the Liberal government in recent years to assist the farmer. I think we have reason to be proud of the system of price supports, credit facilities through the Canadian farm loan board, the freight rate assistance on feed grain and the assistance through the maritime marshland rehabilitation administration, and so on. These measures, and the efficient administration of our economy which brought it to such a level of prosperity, are amongst the main reasons why Canadian farmers, helped by the Liberal government, were able to pull themselves out of the depressed conditions which existed under the last Conservative government from 1930 to 1935.
During the last campaign our Liberal leader, the hon. member for Algoma East, outlined further steps which the Liberal party would strive to take on behalf of the Canadian farmer. This program included a system of deficiency payments to supplement our price support system under wheat, oats, barley, flax and rye. The hon. member for Algoma East also outlined his plan to create a farm loan bank which would take over the whole matter of farm credit financing on the federal level. This farm loan bank would make available at reasonable rates longterm, medium-term and short-term credit to assist the farmers in purchasing the necessary equipment or land to establish healthy economic units. It would have as one of its principal functions the assistance of young farmers in getting established on their own, just as the Veterans' Land Act did, which was established by the Liberal administration in 1945 and which made credit available to ex-servicemen returning to the land.
I think most hon. members with any knowledge of farming will realize that this is one of the most important steps that could be taken to keep our family farms intact, and to assist young Canadians who want to remain on the land. It is also one of the most efficient ways of enabling the farmer to produce at prices which will enable him to compete both on the home market and abroad.
Another item in the Liberal program toward which we are working is legislation to make it easier to improve farm homes. Under the National Housing Act much has been done to assist Canadians to build or purchase adequate housing, but unfortunately

for the farmers most of this housing has been constructed in our towns and cities. It is for this reason we feel it is very important now to take specific steps for the purpose of assisting our farmers to improve their homes or to build new ones if they desire. I am not suggesting specifically how it could be done, but I think either the National Housing Act or a farm loan bank, such as I have outlined, could undertake this task.
Of course one of the most important things a government can do for the farmer is to maintain and expand our markets abroad. I am convinced that the free trade policies outlined by my leader are more likely to assist the farmer in this regard than the return to high tariffs and protection, which is obviously the policy of the Conservative government. We all know that our Canadian farmers-
Would the hon. member permit a question?

After I am through, if you do not mind. We all know that our Canadian farmers can only survive and prosper under conditions of the freest possible international trade. If the present government is going to lead us into a war of restrictions and counterrestrictions with our United States neighbours and other good customers, then it will be our farmers who will suffer. In the maritime provinces assistance should be provided to promote and facilitate the establishment of vegetable canning factories to meet our maritime needs, thus helping to keep for our local farmers an industry which properly belongs to them.
During the 1957 campaign the present Prime Minister proclaimed from one end of the country to the other that he was going to introduce a bill of rights for the Canadian farmer, and that he was going to assure to Canadian farmers a level of income comparable to that of other Canadians. Of course this is an ideal we all want to realize, but I suspect that the Prime Minister is already finding it is easier to make a statement like that on the election platform than to back it up by action. While the Agricultural Stabilization Act introduced at the last session of parliament has not been in force long enough to assess its true value, we do know that it is not meeting the needs of the Minister of Agriculture or doing what the Prime Minister said it would. There have been many complaints from both farm organization and farmers about it. The recent announcements of support prices under certain agricultural products indicate that the government intends to do nothing more than put a distress price under a few agricultural products, and
The Budget-Mr. Michaud that these distress-price supports are likely to be of little value in the face of rising costs.
I was rather surprised when I read that the Prime Minister, speaking in Summerside on February 27, during the last election campaign, said according to a report in the Toronto Daily Star of February 28, 1958, that there is a distress price in Canada below which all agricultural prices cannot fall. Of course all hon. members who have read the Agricultural Stabilization Act will realize that only nine agricultural products receive this support. Producers who want other products protected must convince the government of the need to do so. One such product which is not adequately protected is potatoes. If the Prime Minister believes that this act covers all agricultural products I invite him to announce a price for this year's potato crop which will assure the farmers of New Brunswick a fair price in relation to other products. I would apply these remarks to the potato growers of other provinces, such as Prince Edward Island.
As was said in an editorial in the Charlottetown Guardian on June 7, when the price supports on soya beans were announced:
Surely, no one would claim that soya beans, which have been given protection, mean more to the Canadian economy than potatoes.
In view of the constant fluctuations in the market price of potatoes it is particularly important for producers of this important crop to have some assurance that they will receive a fair price for their crop each year. The Minister of Agriculture is quoted as saying he wanted to be sure that a potato surplus did in fact exist before giving his approval to a floor price. The editorial in the Charlottetown Guardian, to which I referred, concludes:
That ought not to be a difficult thing to ascertain. Our understanding is that the officials who went from here to Ottawa to discuss the problem, told officials that there is a surplus. What need is there for further inquiry?
Earlier this month a delegation from Prince Edward Island, headed by agriculture minister Eugene Cullen, came to Ottawa to urge the government to have potatoes placed under this act. I hope the Minister of Agriculture and his colleagues will soon meet this request. While I am on the subject of price supports I should like to draw the attention of the house to a quotation from the Prime Minister's speech of February 26 last in Rimouski concerning price support for pulpwood. I quote from the Toronto Daily Star of February 27, 1958:

The Budget-Mr. Michaud "I hope (Mr. Diefenbaker said) that the advisory committee and the stabilization board (which administer the price support act) will give consideration to including farm produced woods, so that they will know the lowest price they will receive in a year, in advance."
I am sure all farmers who cut pulpwood on their farms during the winter months will look forward to an early announcement by the government on this subject, especially since the Prime Minister stated in his speech at Rimouski that representations had already been made by the producers to have such price support established.
It is because of the professed interest of the Conservative spokesmen during the election campaign in the welfare of our farmers that we have awaited with interest the government's pronouncements on policy. We were surprised and disappointed to find a contrast between the great promises made on the election platform and the very brief references to the farm economy in the speech from the throne and in the budget address last week. As a matter of fact, the Canadian farmer is certainly the forgotten man as far as this budget is concerned. All this budget means to him is higher prices through protectionist policies, and because the government is doing nothing to fight rising costs.
We had hoped that the government would announce a plan to put into effect its promises concerning the extension of credit to farmers. It is true that there is a bill before the house for the purpose of increasing the resources of the Canadian farm loan board by some $2 million. Is this the completely new deal Canadian farmers have been promised to assist them in obtaining long-term, medium-term and short-term credit? This step is all the more surprising in view of the fact that Conservative candidates throughout the country stated during the campaign that the farm loan board was not the answer to the farm credit problem, and that new steps would be taken.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture must be very disappointed as well. In their brief of June 2 to the government they urged that loans under the farm loan board should be increased to $20,000, and the loan period increased to 40 years. They also urged that the percentage of appraised value of real estate available as a loan be increased, and they urged a reduction in the rate of interest charged. Another recommendation was on a specific system of supervised loans for young farmers and marginal farmers. They also urged that farm improvement loans be made available at a lower interest rate, namely 4J per cent, and that longer periods for repayment of loans on farm machinery should be provided.

Furthermore, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture urges a specific program of emergency loans to help farmers stricken by natural disasters. Such loans should carry no interest unless unnecessary default in payment is shown. Surely this step will recommend itself to the government, because they are on record during the campaign as favouring immediate adoption of a nationwide system of crop insurance, a policy incidentally, which has also been advocated by the Liberal party.
In the same brief to which I have referred the Canadian Federation of Agriculture expresses the hope that something will soon be done to set up such a system of crop insurance. I have stated that the problems facing our farmers are complicated. It was because the former prime minister, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, realized this that he took the important step of having set up the Senate committee on land use. Mr. St. Laurent hoped that the recommendations of this committee would serve as the basis of a new national policy to assist in the preservation of the family farm and to assure the best possible use of our land resources. Unfortunately the Conservative government has shown little enthusiasm for this committee, which has so much to offer to the Canadian farmer. At the last session of parliament I believe it was set up very late in the session and met only a few times. I urge the government to do everything in its power to assist this committee to arrive at its conclusions as early as possible.
In conclusion, I remind the government that it has a solemn commitment to the Canadian farmers, and it is our intention to see that they live up to that commitment.

Mr. Speaker, as I rise today to make my first contribution in this House of Commons I do so with a deep sense of humility, pride and respons-iblity. Responsibility goes with the appointment. That is what I like to call legal authority, without which one's representation would be passive rather than active.

Today as I stand here, Mr. Speaker, I am thinking of a different type of authority, something that is achieved by hard work, built up brick by brick, day by day, the mutual confidence between my constituents, this assembly and myself. This is what I like to call earned authority. It is something we have earned; it cannot be taken away from us. By the same token, you can take it with you as recompense for service performed.
Now, inasmuch as this is my first effort, I would like to take this opportunity to add my warm congratulations to Mr. Speaker on his appointment. I would also like to add my congratulations to the Deputy Speaker and, moreover, to the two gentlemen who moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They did so with dignity and substance, and I think set a standard which has been somewhat difficult to follow.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I look upon this effort of mine today as a sort of prelude to something more at a later date. Since I have been in the House of Commons I have got the impression that a member of parliament coming from a constituency must adopt a different outlook, a national outlook, a broader outlook. I agree, sir, in principle because the heart of parliament is right here in Ottawa. However, we cannot forget the fact that a heart must have arteries, and those arteries must be kept open. If people are to have a say in the government of the day they certainly must be kept in contact.
As a little background, I come from a province which made a clean sweep in the last election. I think it might be of interest to make some deductions on just how the people were thinking and how that achievement came about. Primarily I think we westerners decided that the time had arrived when we must try to keep in tune with the rest of Canada. I think, too, that the Prime Minister had a lot to do with it. His sincerity and ability certainly made the election easier. On top of that, I think the people decided that we must have a strong government nationally and internationally.
To add a little more to the background, I should like to say a few words about my constituency. Red Deer is a city whose growth has been accelerating and continues to do so. It is the centre of one of the most progressive and productive mixed farming districts in Alberta. The constituency encompasses such towns as Innisfail which, incidentally, got a post office last year; Olds, where the school of agriculture is located; Didsbury, which needs a post office; Three Hills, which also got a post office last year;
The Budget-Mr. Rogers Sundre, the gateway to the west where there are fishing, lumbering and oil interests; Rocky Mountain House, farther west again, the gateway to a lumbering region; and Sylvan Lake, a well known summer resort. In passing may I say that I am very happy that the Department of Public Works is spending $40,000 on the pier at Sylvan Lake.
I said that the constituency of Red Deer is a productive and progressive mixed farming district. We are quite proud of some of our breeders who are well known right across the dominion and certainly take their share of honours at the Royal every year. The economy of the constituency is definitely dependent upon agriculture. It is supplemented, it is true, by some oil, lumbering and tourist activities, but basically we are only as prosperous as is agriculture.
Agriculture is the foundation of our country. Western Canada has the distinction of not only growing the highest quality wheat in the world but of being able to produce it at the lowest cost. On the other hand, the wheat growers find that they are dependent on the export market, and in that market they have to compete with countries where the growing of wheat is subsidized. Unfortunately the export market sets the domestic price as	well.	Today	the wheat
growers are selling wheat at away below the cost of production, and something certainly has to be done by way of deficiency payments.
The agricultural	game is so	mixed	up
that it is very difficult to explain. Our farmers are versatile, and when they cannot get a fair price for wheat they go into the raising of stock. But the situation boils down to this fact, that if we do not do something for the wheat grower we will have to do something for the beef producer, and certainly we will have to do something for the dairy producer immediately.
The government	has	moved	rapidly	tomeet the problems of agriculture by providing advances on farm-stored grain and setting up the price stabilization board. These are steps in the right direction but, as I said before, they are not enough and some consideration must be given to the wheat grower. I submit,	Mr.	Speaker, that	the
western wheat growers are the only group who have made any contribution toward meeting inflation. It has been forced, it is true; nevertheless that is a fact.
Apart from the wheat problem, dairying, which plays a very important part in our constituency, would appear to be in for some trouble. Unless additional markets are developed or subsidization is provided, the industry is going to be in serious trouble. There are

The Budget-Mr. Rogers some bright spots such as the beef and swine situations. This is due mainly to the United States market for beef; but with the exception of a group of well to do and more strongly established mixed farmers, agriculture is experiencing one of the most difficult periods in its history. The rural population is urban bound. New, young farmers, caught in the price squeeze before becoming firmly established, are either hanging on by their boot tops or giving up the struggle. Furthermore, older farmers who should retire are unable to do so, and their sons are adding to the difficulties of the unemployment situation.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that measures such as that outlined by the government to provide long term credit, with a minimum ceiling of at least $20,000, would serve a dual purpose. It would give a number of young farmers an opportunity to become firmly established and would put them back on the farms on a fulltime basis instead of being in urban centres looking for employment. Long-term credit would give the older farmer enough cash to move into a town or city and permit his son to carry on the farm.
In this connection I contemplate supervised credit and, if I may be so bold as to say so, in the interests of economy and sound administration I suggest that such credit facilities should be administered by the director of the Veterans' Land Act administration. I have a reason for making this suggestion. I worked with the Veterans' Land Act administration for a number of years, and I can say first of all that they have field men strategically located across our great dominion. A second factor is that the work under the Veterans' Land Act has reached its peak. I think it will go down from now on, and there is no reason why the staff should not be maintained.
No better job could be given to them than that of supervising such credit. The important factor about such a move is that these field men are experienced. They are accredited appraisers, but above all they are willing and anxious to work as a team with the borrower and his family. They are not merely men interested in routine. They give everything they have to their job. They are interested in citizenship and not simply the farm. I could not be stronger in my recommendation that when a supervised long-term credit scheme is established it should be administered by the Veterans' Land Act officials.
I was amazed at the preceding speaker expounding what the former Liberal administration had done for the farmers. I think this government can take a lot of credit for what has been done. I should like to read a few extracts from The Organized Farmer, the monthly publication of the farmers' union

of Alberta. This is the organ or the mouthpiece of the Farmers' Union of Alberta, a non-political organization, an organization that likes to think it represents the farmers and in the main does so. I quote:
About one year ago now the farm union sent a large and representative farm delegation to Ottawa to press for government action to help solve the farm problem. The welcome mat was not noticeable when we arrived. The then Prime Minister was too busy to see us. I think that when we left Ottawa it was the opinion of most that we had convinced members of parliament that there was a farm problem, but few of us believed that we would see much done about our program in the near future.
What does this say? This is speaking of the Conservative government:
Yes, it has been a year of solid accomplishments. Those who took part in the delegation, those who served as information officers in Ottawa, those members of parliament and of government who supported our program, those local people who helped design the program, and those who have canvassed year after year and worked hard to keep our organization going, and the plain ordinary member who contributed only money-all these deserve credit for the job that has been done-
Despite long hours in the house, in cabinet meetings, and in the administration of their departments, we have always had an opportunity to present our case. Sometimes it has been late at night and other unorthodox hours, but always we have had a hearing. It would have been easy for them to have avoided these sessions but they did not choose to do so-*
It is in such an environment that farm problems can be solved. If government and farmer continue to work hard, and work together, as they are learning to do, then the great problems of agriculture can be solved and we can have the kind of agriculture that we farmers have been working for these many years.
I submit that that is a different attitude from that of the previous administration. It is not the whole answer. The trend is there. There is a definite indication that this government is preparing to work with the farmers, the backbone of this country. I may say they saved us in two wars and will probably save us in another one. That is why we must look after this industry.
There is another problem that is facing this country. I refer to the burden of taxation on our municipalities. I believe that the municipalities in the province of Alberta have the second largest per capita debt in the Dominion of Canada. With the accelerated growth in certain cities the burden of replacing and extending facilities has reached a point where something must be done to equalize the tax structure. I am pleased to note that the budget offers some relief in this regard. However, I am sure that the ordinary land owner and the ordinary taxpayer are looking to the proposed conference of the municipalities with the federal government in September when it is hoped that,

after a full analysis has been made, a way will be found for a fairer and sounder equalization of taxes.
Since I have been in this House of Commons unemployment has been the key subject of discussion. I submit that this is a problem that affects us all. However, I do not know whether talking about it is going to do much good. The funny thing about unemployment is that it seems to create a fear in people who have work. They want more work. I think this is not only a problem of the government and of the opposition parties but of every Canadian as long as one fellow Canadian is without work. It will not do much good to tell the government about the unemployment situation. This is the responsibility of every Canadian in Canada and I am not so sure that every Canadian in Canada is doing too much about it.
For instance, I know of certain Canadians who have three jobs and whose earnings are increased to the extent that they are earning more than their boss, in the amount of $8,500. There seems to be a grabbing fear that strikes Canadians when unemployment hits and they seem to say: "Let's get all the money we can get". I maintain that if we can provide one job for one household we shall be doing a fairly good job. If we have any feeling at all for our fellow Canadians, I think that is what we should try to do.
Public works are going to set a pattern to help out the unemployment situation. But I think it is up to the leaders of industry and the leaders of labour to make a survey in order to find out just how people are working; and if they have three jobs or two jobs when one is sufficient, I think we shall have to take a stand somewhere and say, "One job for one".
Certain things can be done by the government. In Red Deer our number of unemployed was the largest in history last year; at that time some 2,100 were unemployed. The situation has improved considerably since that time and I am told that it is expected that the situation will be rectified. However, as far as my constituency is concerned, I am not so much disturbed about this summer because I believe most people will be put to work. On the other hand, we are all worried about the recurrence of unemployment next fall.
As I said before, our economy is dependent upon agriculture. If agriculture goes down, then the rest go down with it. If it is prosperous, we prosper as well. In other words, we farm the farmer. We need secondary industries. We have growing suspicions that many of these small industries coming to this country are sidestepped to
The Budget-Mr. Rogers the east when in fact they should be sent out west where, in respect of living conditions, they would have much more in common with the place they left. I know that we must have secondary industry. No matter how we get it we shall have to get it. That would help.
The second factor is this. The government, through their public works, could be of assistance. This has been put up to me by construction contractors because I made a survey before I came down here. They say that if public works would let their contracts in the fall for spring contracts it would mean employing a number of men because these same contractors would have something firm on which to work. They could hold more of their staff, get their machinery in shape and do certain things such as brushing, moving rocks and so on. In any case they have staff there which they are reluctant to let go and if they have any excuse at all they would hang on to them and give them something to do whereas, under the present plan, where they have not a contract and do not know if they are ever going to get one, the work does not start until about the end of June. There are many measures which could be taken to improve this situation.
The unemployment situation has caused great concern to the people of Canada and this problem is not going to be settled merely by talk. We have to do something about it and if we face the facts I think we must do something about it.
So much for local problems, and now I would like to commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on his presentation of the budget. The minister's ability to formulate and present facts in proper sequence was indeed a revelation to me. No thinking Canadian expected much tax relief and it was therefore refreshing to witness the courage and wisdom of the minister in bringing down a realistic budget well suited to the difficult problems which exist in our country today. One of the most important functions of government is the bringing down of the budget and I believe that the minister, in bringing down his budget as quickly as he did, has provided a much needed stimulant for our economy.
It was simply not possible to provide more relief by way of tax reduction, but it is only human nature to hold back from making purchases in the hope of such tax relief being afforded. The budget does, however, offer some relief to the ordinary Canadian in respect of assistance to municipalities and to farmers and has provided an incentive for exploration and development to be carried

The Budget-Mr. Rogers out by the oil industry. There are many other smaller concessions and some measures which should appeal to all Canadians. I particularly have in mind the estate tax replacing the present succession duty. This measure will provide great relief to widows, allowing them an exemption up to $60,000 with an additional amount for each of three children. Estate duty has been a matter of great concern to many of our countrymen and as a matter of fact before the budget was brought down I had received five letters on this subject.
The proposed amendment to section 35 of the Customs Act in order to stop unfair dumping of foreign goods will also relieve much hardship. Of course it is true that our industry must stand up to reasonable competition. Competition is the lifeblood of trade but to allow dumping is an entirely different question and is certainly unfair to industry and labour in Canada.
The amendment to the Income Tax Act in order to allow corporations to make gifts of up to 10 per cent of income, the intention being to increase the flow of money from these sources to higher education, will I know considerably help the universities. Their need is most apparent and this will provide an overdue boost for them.
As a new member of the house I must say the criticism advanced thus far by the opposition has been totally unreasonable and is just a smoke screen to hide the facts. Opposition members condemn the deficit budget but imply, on the other hand, that the budget does not go far enough in order to get industry in motion and thus relieve our unemployment situation. Of course you cannot have it both ways. It would not be courteous or, for that matter, prudent for me to say too much with respect to this criticism but so far as I am concerned nothing can beat democracy. However, to judge from the proceedings in this house democracy is certainly a slow grinding process. I suppose one gets accustomed to it and I hope I will. We have reached the point in our history where we must decide whether we will continue to be a producer of raw materials or whether we shall process those raw materials.
This is no time for complacency; there are vital problems to be solved and an appropriate part must be played not only by the government but by the opposition parties and the leaders of industry and labour in the solving of these problems and in the advancement of our culture. I submit that anything less is a betrayal of our fellow Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the various presentations in this debate and I think the greatest commendation of the proposals advanced by the C.C.F. group, outlined in our subamendment, came from those sitting on the government benches. There was one slight exception, but as I have listened to the speeches and have read Hansard I have not found one instance of any government member opposing the subject matter contained in that subamendment. The exception, of course, was when the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Macdonnell) in a very gracious way made reference to the speech of the leader of the C.C.F. as free-wheeling, gassy and windy. However, he did not go into any detail with respect to his remarks.
It is therefore obvious at least from the silence of hon. members opposite, that there is plenty of support for the subamendment which we placed before this house. I predict, of course, that if and when a vote is taken the government will not dare to allow a free vote on it. In fact, following the lead of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) when he was in opposition, I would go so far as to challenge the government to undertake that there will be such a free vote, and if that is done, it should not be considered a motion of want of confidence. I make this request just as the Minister of Finance used to do when he sat on this side of the house, but I am sure that neither he nor the government will undertake to accept this particular challenge, for they know just as well as I do the surprise that would be experienced when the result of the vote was made known.
Before we get into too much detail on the budget itself, there is one subject I should like to mention; one that may be considered rather a delicate topic for a member to raise publicly, especially so soon after an election. But I understand from reading newspaper reports that some of the newly elected members of this house, members who were elected under the auspices of the Conservative party, have expressed some ideas and opinions on this matter, though so far in this house I have not heard much about it. I refer to the indemnity structure provided for members of parliament. While this may be considered an impractical thing to discuss, and while it may also be a politically unwise subject to discuss, because certainly we are one of the few groups in society which could be accused of increasing its own salaries, I should like to pursue this matter a little further.
I am not dealing with this question of increasing the indemnity. I should like to

deal with the inequalities which at present exist in the structure of the indemnity as it relates to members from urban areas as against members from rural areas. As any hon. member knows who represents a rural constituency-one which covers many, many square miles; in some cases, thousands of square miles-great cost is involved in attempting to get around such extensive areas and in keeping in touch with the various organizations in the small communities throughout the constituency either personally or by telephone. Skeena, for instance, has an area of about 127,000 square miles, which constitutes almost one-third of the entire area of the province of British Columbia. In fact you could put the whole three maritime provinces twice over into the constituency of Skeena and still have room for a fairly large area for an hon. member to represent.

In the course of last session we had what was classified as a baby budget in which a few changes were made in the fiscal policy of the government. I should like to deal with one of these in particular. During that session the Minister of Finance introduced an amendment to the Income Tax Act to provide for some relief for construction workers as
The Budget-Mr. Howard far as income tax is concerned. That in itself was a fair and just change to have made, but I would say that all it did was merely to aggravate what was already a discriminatory provision of the Income Tax Act and worsen it by making a change affecting one group of workmen and not others who are similarly placed. I refer, of course, to the logging section of the lumber industry on the coast of British Columbia, to loggers in other parts of the country and to other employees who are in exactly the same position as construction workers inasmuch as they have to leave their places of residence and go to some other part of the country to realize an income.
When this matter was raised last session the Minister of Finance said at that time that the only representations that had ever been made to the government for changes in this respect related to construction workers. Of course, it was brought to his attention that such was not the case and that other representations had been made to the previous Liberal administration about this matter, and the hope was expressed that the minister would look at the representations which were made to the previous administration and bring in additional changes to the act this year. That is one of the major complaints I have to make concerning the attitude of the Minister of Finance as compared with the position he took last session. I have the honour to be a member of one of the locals of the International Woodworkers of America in British Columbia which over the years has been greatly concerned about this discriminatory feature in the Income Tax Act and which has made continuous representations not only to the Minister of Finance but to members of the House of Commons in previous parliaments about the changes which were thought necessary.
As some hon. members may be aware, loggers, particularly on the coast of British Columbia, spend seven, eight, nine or ten months maybe, depending on the area in which they are working, away from their homes. Weather conditions on the coast of British Columbia necessitate at least twice during the year the loggers being laid off from their employment and having to pay the cost of transportation back to their own homes, and these homes are normally in the lower mainland. When conditions allow for the resumption of work in the logging industry they have to pay their fares back to camp in order to start work again. In the winter time heavy snow on the coast of British Columbia tends to shut down work, and in the summer, because of the hot dry weather-as is likely to be the case this year, and as was the case particularly in 1951- other shut-downs take place. So the men

The Budget-Mr. Howard have to pack their bags or suitcases, pack their hard hats and caulked boots and head back to Vancouver.
In terms of the money a man has to expend out of his own pocket for fares to get to these logging camps, that varies from $1 to $2 for logging camps near Vancouver up to $100 or $125 for logging camps farther up the coast.
The board and lodging charges are also extra burdens. We have been asking for years and years to have changes made in the Income Tax Act to allow loggers to deduct the amount they spend for board and lodging charges in camps, especially when these loggers are maintaining a home and family in some other part of the province. This means they are maintaining a second home in the bunkhouse where they live while they are working. Some adjustment should be made in the income tax provisions as they apply to this type of worker. I mention loggers particularly because I know them. I have worked in the logging industry and I know the problems that they have quite intimately. The mere fact that I have not mentioned in detail other working people who are similarly situated does not mean that I do not have the same amount of sympathy for their problems as I do for the loggers. I can only hope at the moment that some time in the future the Minister of Finance will undertake to make this long overdue and very necessary change.
There is another question of discrimination which arises out of this particular budget, and which has been in effect for many years. I have often wondered if there was any connection betwen the word "Tory" and the word "discriminatory". I see by looking at this budget that it is quite easy to draw that inference, and that is probably how the pseudonym of "Tory" came about in the first place. For many years the coast of British Columbia has been discriminated against, as compared with the Atlantic coast, when it comes to assistance for shipping facilities, for passenger and freight services. I am not implying in any way that the assistance given to the Atlantic provinces for shipping facilities should not be given. I am merely pointing out the great difference in attitude that has been evidenced in past governments, and this one as well, in connection with shipping on the British Columbia coast as compared with shipping and passenger facilities on the Atlantic coast.
How many millions of dollars have been spent in years past in either acquiring or building vessels for the east coast, and in payments of subventions to shipping on that coast, I do not know. The amount could be


determined, I imagine, by totalling the figures in the various estimates during the years past. However, the amount of money that British Columbia obtains for the same type of service, passenger service and freight shipping facilities, is a mere pittance when compared to the amount which has been given to provinces along the Atlantic. This year, for instance, in direct payment from the Department of Transport for the construction and acquisition of vessels for use along the Atlantic coasts and for subventions or subsidy payments to Atlantic shipping, the Atlantic provinces are obtaining a little less than $5.25 million, compared with the amount allocated for subventions for shipping on the British Columbia coast of about $332,000. This means that about 15 times more money has been allocated to the same service on the Atlantic coast than has been allocated to services along the Pacific coast.
Passenger service by ship along the coast of British Columbia has deteriorated. Some years ago the service was not too bad. There were adequate facilities serving the small communities and logging camps. However, the attitude of the government has been to leave coastal shipping service along the coast of British Columbia in the hands of some fly-by-night, two-bit ship operators who are not concerned with providing service but merely concerned with travelling to the most lucrative areas and charging whatever rate they can get. These shipping companies in British Columbia gradually deteriorated and many of them have gone out of business because they were trying to cut corners on costs or because they did not know what they were doing which resulted in ships piling up on rocks, with loss of lives and the ships themselves ruined beyond the possibility of reconstruction. I am not referring to the strike that is now in effect against the Canadian Pacific because it only covers a small portion of the shipping lanes along the coast of British Columbia, the area between Vancouver and Vancouver island and one run up the coast. This strike is something which arises out of labour-management negotiations. However, if subsidies are necessary in order to maintain the operation of these vessels, then subsidies should be granted just as they are granted in many cases to shipping companies along the Atlantic provinces.
The only solution to this problem, and the one which we have advocated for many years now with regard to shipping on the coast of British Columbia, is operation by a crown corporation. In this way we would ensure that adequate facilities are provided and that service could be curtailed or increased when necessary. If the shipping facilities along

the coast of British Columbia were under one crown corporation, the entire operation could be co-ordinated so that the profitable runs would be able, to some degree if not completely, to offset the non-profitable runs and the runs which must necessarily be put into effect in order to provide service first. We could worry about profit and loss statements afterwards. We are asking for fair treatment in this regard.
An important deficiency in the budget, apart from the fact that the major problem throughout the nation is one of unemployment, is the failure of the budget to take any cognizance of the high personal taxation that is in existence today and which has been in existence for some time. Some of us had the privilege of hearing about unemployment today from a delegation of unemployed who appeared in the railway committee room and who came from various parts of Ontario. I refer to this high personal taxation not because it affects everyone but because it reflects the insincerity of this government. If one wishes to arrive at a decision in this regard, he only has to compare the many speeches and the pages of Hansard that hon. members opposite used to fill when they sat on this side of the house and the election promises that they made both before this last election and before the one in 1957 as to what this Tory group would do if they ever got into office when it came to reducing income taxes or increasing exemptions, and compare that with the budget. As you well know, Mr. Speaker, that is the subject matter of the subamendment now before us.
Whenever I want something amusing to read I can always find it by reading the annual presentation the Minister of Finance made when he was sitting on this side of the house. I am sure if he has a few hours to spare from his regular 18-hour day, if he would re-read some of these speeches he made when he sat over here they might prick his conscience a little bit and make him realize the necessity for making this adjustment in the personal income tax and increasing the exemptions, which course he so loudly espoused not many months ago, to $1,500 for single people and $3,000 for married people.
We know that election promises are easy to come by. We know that prior to 1957 the Conservatives had all sorts of fanciful promises to make; we also know that it is now quite obvious they had no intention of keeping them. Whether I can, I do not think I should make any reference to the integrity of the Minister of Finance because I know that even though he appears to be reading he has one ear cocked on the words that are issuing forth from this corner and would be only too quick to jump to his feet-

Well, of course, I thought that is what a Minister of Finance was employed for, to find answers to those questions; but if you want the answers from the opposition we are more than willing to give you the benefit of our knowledge, knowing full well that one of these days the party opposite will become as desirous of pilfering sections from the program of some other parties as the Liberals were when they were in office. When that time comes we shall be pleased to give you more suggestions and pleased to see you accept them.
But there are one or two inequities which exist in the taxation legislation of this country which have been brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance on many occasions. It would not do any harm to have them brought to his attention again today. In the first place, this is the most iniquitous one. It relates to the portion of our income tax which goes into the old age security fund for the payment of old age pensions, the so-called 2-2-2 formula. The two per cent personal income tax has a ceiling of $60 placed on it. This is one place where we suggest the minister could get the additional income. He should connect the all-inclusive payment of old age pensions, which means that they are received without any means test, with payment without any means test and remove the ceiling of $60 payments to the old age 

security fund. Based on the 1955 taxation statistics this would probably mean an additional $20 million.
If we were to return to the percentage of corporation tax that was charged a few years ago we could realize an additional $112 million to $115 million of income based on 1955 statistics. The 20 per cent tax dividend which gives a legal tax dodge to some people who get their income in a certain way should be done away with and it would give us even more. So far as the capital gains tax is concerned I know the minister opposes it if he has not changed his mind since he was in opposition. He has changed it on a great many other things, but I doubt whether he has changed it on this. How much money we could receive in income from a capital gains tax is more than I know. There are no statistics available. There is no breakdown in the taxation statistics or anywhere else, at least that I have been able to find, as to the amount of income available from a capital gains tax.
One of the most perplexing things that I have tried to do is to attempt to classify this budget and what terms we could apply to it.
Glowing.

I have not used the word
glowing in this anagram that I have drawn up, but I have picked another word starting with "g" that makes it even more acceptable. But there is a better way to immortalize the name of the father of the budget and that is by using the initials of his last name in drawing up a number of adjectives to apply to the budget. Let us run down the letters which make up his last name. We find that we can very easily define it as "fleecing", "limp",-
Lovely.

"Empty", "mean", "mercenary", "insincere", "nauseating" and the last one is "greedy"; "iniquitous" is another one for you. Fleecing, because it continues to exact a heavy toll from individual taxpayers and still robs the man in the lower income group; limp, because the natural milk of human kindness, which farmers particularly need, has been left out of the recipe; empty, because it is empty of any principle or philosophy except the principle of meanness, meanness to old age pensioners, retired civil servants, retired railway employees and others in similar fixed income groups; insincere, because it obviously abandons and has no connection whatsoever with election promises or with the comments hon. gentlemen used to make when they sat over here; nauseating, because it rebuffs the legitimate request for food in the stomachs of the unemployed and their

families; greedy, because it obviously means more and more cost without any concomitant amount of services related thereto.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like through you to convey my best wishes, and I hope the best wishes of the house, to the Canadian nursing association for the successful convention they are holding. I should like to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on his most difficult task in explaining so clearly the economic aspects of the country resulting in the budget we have had presented to us. To inherit the very difficult mantle of the finance ministry even at the best of times assures one of some unpopularity with the taxpayers, no matter how generous the minister in question may be, but to have assumed this role during a time of economic recession makes the task even more arduous since the minister must walk the knife edge between recession and inflation.
The opposition members, particularly those who so recently occupied this side of the house, have called the budget a blue budget and they have criticized the minister for not reducing taxes more as they would have done, so they say. I would think they would be more grateful in that they now may write off their expenses for eye glasses because that party has had a reputation for shortsightedness for some time. I should like to assure the opposition that the Canadian people are not too easily fooled by these cries of distress. If there were an opportunity in the very near future the result at the polls might be even more devastating than it was on March 31.
