subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR SECRECY AND DESTRUCTION OF REPORTS, ETC.
AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR SECRECY AND DESTRUCTION OF REPORTS, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-20, to amend the Juvenile Delinquents Act.

He said: As stated in the explanatory notes, the purpose of the amendment suggested by this bill is to provide for the absolute secrecy of reports, files and records in connection with the trial of juvenile delinquents and to provide further that such records and files be destroyed after a period of five years from the date of such trial. I do submit, Mr. Speaker, that this amendment meets a social need and, in addition, is in accordance with the spirit of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. Indeed, subsection 2 of section 3 is enacted in the following terms:
When a child is adjudged to have committed a delinquency he shall be dealt with, not as an offender, but as one in a condition of deliquency and therefore requiring help and guidance and proper supervision.
Section 38 underlines still more the legislature's intent in the following terms:
This act shall be liberally construed to the end that its purpose may be carried out, namely that the care and custody and discipline of a juvenile delinquent shall approximate as nearly as may be that which should be given by its parents, and that as far as practicable every juvenile delinquent shall be treated, not as a criminal, but as a misdirected and misguided child, and one needing aid, encouragement, help and assistance.
These two sections are all the more important as they are inspired by the factors and conditions which contribute to juvenile delinquency.
Obviously these factors are numerous and manifold. But one of the most important is surely the family's conditions. In a work entitled "The Juvenile Offender", published some years ago, Professor Clyde B. Vedder, of the University of Florida, stresses the influence of home and family in the following terms:
It cannot be overemphasized that a child's family is the most important influence in shaping his personality and character. In this profound primary group the child acquires his basic ideals and a sense of right and wrong. Here he first experiences social interaction and becomes conscious of standards, goals, values and the formulation of judgments. Here he is a member of the allunit of society, the first stage upon which he learns to imitate his elders as he begins his awakening into a fuller knowledge of the world about him.
The general purpose of the Juvenile Delinquents Act is precisely to give to the child who is the victim of his environment the help and guidance and the proper supervision which he did not find within his own family. In his very interesting work entitled, "Belief and Action", Viscount Samuel recalls the psychological fact that:
Among the ordinary supports of morals in everyday life we may see that habit is of the first importance. The normal person is not constantly reflecting whether he shall be honest or not; he is honest by habit and as a matter of course.
In order to root this habit in his conscience, the juvenile delinquent should be treated not 57071-3-I00J
Juvenile Delinquents Act as a criminal but as a misdirected and misguided child. In its summary of recommendations, the committee appointed to inquire into the remission service of the Department of Justice of Canada recalls this fundamental rule with respect to the administration of justice:
Some means should be found whereby the courts, at all levels, may be made more conscious that the purpose of punishment is the correction of the offender and not mere retribution by society.
This truth is especially to the point when the offender is a youth and, generally speaking, is not truly the only one responsible for his conduct. It follows that society has no right to give him harmful publicity and still less to make him carry a police record through his life like a millstone around his neck.
In my professional practice I have sometimes had the opportunity to note how unscrupulous are certain organizations. I have in mind particularly those companies whose business it is to make investigations for the benefit of certain finance or insurance corporations. Even in the army it does happen that an old record of a former juvenile delinquent is a handicap to his promotion in spite of the fact that his present conduct and qualifications are excellent.
Twelve years ago in the district of Quebec there was formed a social service to work for the rehabilitation of juvenile delinquents. Since that time this organization has rendered great services to our society and in October of 1956 at the conclusion of a symposium, many resolutions were passed, two of which I would like to quote as follows:
(Translation):
3. This meeting wonders whether an adult considered as rehabilitated, who has given proof of good behaviour during a period recognized as long enough to dispel any fear of relapse, should benefit from a privilege on the part of the authorities, concerning the existence of a police record.
And then, number 7:
7. Dr. Gauthier suggests that the records of young delinquents do not constitute in any way for them a true police record and that they should not be revealed to any individual nor any society.
(Text):
My suggestion to this house was in fact inspired by those resolutions. As a result of the proposed amendment anyone not engaged in the administration of justice or in the rehabilitation of juvenile delinquents will be denied access to existing records. Moreover, after a period of five years from the date of the trial of any juvenile delinquent his or her records and files would be destroyed so that he or she will really feel a normal citizen who henceforth has the

Juvenile Delinquents Act right to a free and complete existence in society, rather than being considered as some sort of untouchable.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR SECRECY AND DESTRUCTION OF REPORTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel I have some justification in rising to speak to this bill because I have spent some five years in juvenile and family court work. I am entirely in favour of the principle of the bill which would make the records of juveniles inaccessible to the general public, to the magistrates' courts or indeed to any persons other than to officials of the juvenile courts themselves.
There are two principles involved in this bill, as a matter of fact, firstly with respect to the availability of the records to other authorities and, secondly, with respect to the destruction of those records when they have completed their usefulness to court authorities.
Many juveniles appear before juvenile courts today who would not formerly have done so. Many offences brought before juvenile and family courts are of a very minor character and the authorities take this course in order to draw the attention of parents, teachers and the juveniles themselves to the fact that these children have got slightly out of line with the accepted practices in the adult world.
As the member who introduced the bill has stated, the juvenile delinquent is no longer treated as a criminal but is now treated as a person having need of special care and assistance in the hope that he or she will eventually become a useful citizen.
Before the Juvenile Delinquents Act came into effect juveniles who got into difficulties were brought before magistrates, with some very undesirable results. In the first place the provisions of the Criminal Code stated that juvenile cases must be heard last and that the court must be cleared. This resulted in many instances of juveniles, brought to court for minor offences, having to sit in court for at least part of an afternoon listening to the sordid stories told in magistrates' courts. This may have resulted in the juvenile's education having been widened but I believe the knowledge of adult delinquencies would be harmful to these children.
Since the Juvenile Delinquents Act has been in force and its application has become more widespread throughout the country, it has been proclaimed throughout the different jurisdictions and people are now becoming more familiar with the procedure in bringing children before juvenile and family courts. The jurisdiction of the magistrate was very limited before the introduction of this
[Mr. Dorion.l
legislation. He was limited to dismissing the charge against the child or placing him on suspended sentence or fining him. In these circumstances, a large number of very minor offences were never brought to the attention of the authorities and as a result the juvenile felt he had got away with whatever he was doing and was left with some disposition to try it again. Perhaps on the second occasion it became a much more serious affair and the very benefit of what he might have received in the first instance was gone.
I would turn up, if I may, section 20 of the Juvenile Delinquents Act as it now stands to indicate the type of punishment, if it can be called that, which a juvenile court can now impose on a juvenile. First, it can suspend final disposition. This type of disposal of a case is most often used where a juvenile has become involved in some very minor offence. Suspending final disposition shelves a matter as effectively, in fact as it is sometimes shelved in this house by sending questions to committees or some other place. Suspension of final disposition is used quite often, but there is nevertheless a record that a particular juvenile has been brought before a court and found guilty of some offence even though that offence may be minor in character-it might be nothing more serious than riding a bicycle on a sidewalk contrary to some local by-law although it could also be something more serious in connection with the transgression of a provincial or federal statute. But regardless of these distinctions it must be a minor matter, and the whole affair is passed over, and as far as the courts are concerned, forgotten.
This, I think, is the main type of case which the hon. member who introduced the bill is trying to protect. These are the children who have stepped out of line once, as all of us have done at some time before reaching maturity and becoming acquainted with the standards which the people of this country expect from adult persons. In these circumstances I think it would be most unfair for a record of such a juvenile to be kept and held against him as what one might call a criminal record.
These children are brought before the juvenile courts nowadays at any age after they have reached the age of understanding. I have known them to be brought before the courts at the age of eight or nine years where there has been a serious infraction of the law. The law would not normally expect these children to understand the seriousness of their acts, nevertheless it has been something sufficiently serious to make it necessary for some action to be taken. In this particular type of case I think it is only fair that two things should happen: first, that the record should

eventually be destroyed and, secondly, that the juvenile involved should know that the record is being destroyed.
One of the things which cause second offences as far as many of the authorities are concerned is the fact that when a person has been found guilty and convicted of some offence he feels that that is against him for the rest of his life, and for that reason he may not find it very difficult to go out and commit another offence. But if he could feel that though he had transgressed to some extent the laws of the country while he was small, he had been forgiven by the public; if he could feel that there was that much understanding among the authorities of this country, and that his slip would never be held against him when he had reached maturity, then I think there would be a much greater incentive for that juvenile to try to forget his little slip completely, having in mind that it is not engraved permanently on the court records.
Another thing. Quite often I have found that these juvenile court records were being improperly used by police, magistrates and other persons concerned with the administration of justice. The basic idea behind the Juvenile Delinquents Act is that these juveniles shall be considered as persons in need of help. There are very strict rules governing juvenile courts which say that no names shall be published in the newspapers and that no publicity shall be given to juvenile cases. This is all intended to serve one end, namely that a juvenile who has committed a minor offence shall be allowed to recover without the stigma of a record. Yet there have been many instances where police have gained access to these records in some way or another and have immediately become prejudiced against a particular child, even though he might have been only 11 or 12 years old at the time he committed the offence.
Likewise, as the law presently stands, there is nothing to prevent a record being passed from a juvenile court to an adult court and there held against a defendent. This, again, is not what was intended by the Juvenile Delinquents Act. In some provinces magistrates are men with legal training, but in many provinces they are not, and these records are very important as far as the security of cases is concerned. I am not sure, offhand, that there is any province which requires that a magistrate should be a man with legal training, but in any case, having before him the record of a juvenile who has been in trouble before might give a magistrate the feeling that perhaps the boy has a predisposition for
Juvenile Delinquents Act getting into trouble and that therefore he should be taught a good lesson. I say that these records should not pass into the hands of an adult authority once a boy has reached the age of 16, at least in the province of Ontario-it is 18 in some other provinces- the age when he becomes an adult in the eyes of the law.
There are several other dispensations that juvenile and family court judges may make of a juvenile court case. They may adjourn the hearing for an indefinite period. So far as the criminal law is concerned this is a definite departure from previous well-established principle which states that no criminal case can be adjourned sine die. Under the Juvenile Delinquents Act this can be done, and in many cases an adjournment without a further date being specified is a form of suspended sentence.
Then, thirdly, the judge of the juvenik court may impose a fine not exceeding $25 which may be paid in periodical amounts or otherwise. The use of a fine is quite common. In some cases it is found to be quite useful punishment if a child is made to pay for some damage he has done, that is malicious damage to property such as breaking windows or even knocking the glass insulators off telephone and telegraph poles. They do not realize that these things cost money. However, if there is a fine imposed and the child is ordered to pay that fine himself within a stated period he can often be persuaded, with the co-operation of his parents, to do a certain amount of extra work and by the time he has paid off a fine of $25 for breaking windows he may not find that a suitable occupation in the future.
However, Mr. Speaker, these are things that all of us have done, but we have not all been caught. All of us during our youth I think, have been involved in some such things as breaking windows, and even more serious vandalism, when involved with a group of people or a gang that is bent on making trouble. Yet the Juvenile Delinquents Act recognizes that these boys are not basically bad and that when they have reached the age of maturity they will learn better. It is with that in mind that the limitations have been placed on what can be done with children.
There is another penalty that the juvenile courts can impose, and that is to commit the child to the care of a probation officer. This practice is becoming more and more prevalent in the provinces of Canada. I can speak mainly for the province of Ontario because that is the province in which I was involved. This province is building up a very effective probation service, both for juveniles and adults. It has come into being within the last

Juvenile Delinquents Act seven or eight years. I believe that the person most responsible for it was the Reverend Dan Coughlan, who was taken into the department of the attorney general and given a job to do. He has done that job. The probation service in Ontario is now at its peak. Probation is provided for both adults and juveniles, but at the moment we are concerned with juveniles. If a judge believes a child is running into difficulty because of the neglect of his parents, he can place him directly under the control of a probation officer. In most such cases the probation officer requires reporting and so forth, and keeps an eye on the boy to see that he does not get into any trouble.
In most cases, these children are left in their homes and they are ordered to report to the Children's Aid Society or to a probation officer. The court can also place such children in foster homes, if these children are not being properly looked after at home. They may be placed in the care of the Children's Aid Society.
Again in this case the court is recognizing the fact that it is not the child's fault but the fault of the parents when he is taken from his own home and placed with some one else or with the Children's Aid Society. It has often been said that there are more delinquent parents than there are delinquent children, and I think there is a lot of truth in the statement. A good many children find themselves in difficulty before they reach an age of understanding because the parents have merely neglected to give them any assistance, rather than by reason of the fact the parents have led them into any path of misdoing. Regardless of whether it is the result of neglect or malicious bad example on the part of the parents, it is recognized that it is not the child's fault. In such a case, again, we come back to the same principle that when the child reaches an age of understanding he should not have all these childhood things to cope with and have prejudice created in the mind of the public.
In closing on this question of penalty, I might say there are some cases of a very serious nature. There are cases of boys, of the age of 15, who have not reached adult age, but who have become involved in armed violence. There have been a few involved in cases of murder. In these cases, no matter how serious the offence, they are still within the jurisdiction of the juvenile court. If the juvenile court feels that these cases should be dealt with in the adult court, then the judge has authority to send the case on. Having sent it on to the adult court, it then becomes a matter of record in such adult court. In that case there is no particular reason for

holding back the records. This particular section of the Juvenile Delinquents Act would not apply.
With that background, Mr. Speaker, I would just take a couple of minutes to deal with the two principles involved. The amendment to section 12 of the act provides in general terms that no one who has had the custody or control of a juvenile delinquent, and no one who has charge of the records, shall communicate the contents of those records to any other person not a judge, magistrate, probation officer, superintendent or other officer connected with the administration of justice. I think, to a large extent, this practice is now followed in most of the courts, but that is purely an administrative matter. In other words, those people who have had experience in juvenile work are well acquainted with the fact that some agencies would use these records to the disadvantage of the individual, particularly in so far as employment is concerned. If a young lad were to apply for employment and his employers were permitted to go into the juvenile court record and find he was involved in something serious,-at the moment it is up to the judge to decide whether or not that information should be released. Under this amendment there would be no such jurisdiction and the records would remain private.
Then there is the other principle involved in the later destruction of the records. Again, I feel that is a good provision. The child who has been misled or who has got into difficulty must have the feeling that he did it when he was a boy, that he has been forgiven and that he may now go ahead and live a normal adult life, without the stigma of a childhood prank being held over him for the rest of his life. For all of these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am very much in favour of this bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR SECRECY AND DESTRUCTION OF REPORTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member who has preceded me, the member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken), I have had some experience in dealing with juvenile delinquents in my capacity as crown attorney for the county of Pontiac, which position I held for eight years. As crown attorney, juvenile delinquents were a constant problem and decisions had to be reached concerning those persons. I find that among police officials there is always-and rightly so-a very great reluctance to initiate any kind of proceeding against a juvenile. By that I mean should a complaint be received against a juvenile and that juvenile had never been the object of a complaint before, the police will in most instances, unless the charge is extremely serious, go to the home of the young person involved and question him and his parents.

If the offence is not serious, and if there seems to be satisfactory evidence that such an offence will not be committed again, then the police officer, the social welfare officer or the juvenile delinquent's court officer will simply shelve the complaint and recommend to the parents that closer supervision be kept of the youngster concerned and also the youngster himself in most instances will be reprimanded. Unless the youngster has a long background of delinquent tendencies he will have learned his lesson and never again will he be the object of police investigation.
In other cases the police must proceed to lodge a complaint under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, or even under the Criminal Code, if the offence is more serious. There are two types of juveniles who appear before the courts and they may perhaps be classified in three broad categories. The first are offences of violence, 1 might say, such as assaults, lights, damage to property. The second category is the juvenile who indulges in petty thievery, and the third type deals mostly with delinquents who have been guilty of some sexual perversion.
In the first type of delinquent we find more or less a complex of violence; it is a matter of a young bully who wishes to impose his will by violence upon other youngsters or even in rising against established order and destroying property.
In the case of petty thieves, they are mostly drawn from a background of underprivileged families whose parents may be drunkards or may have separated and who have domestic difficulties and who have developed a resentment against society. They have come to the point where they cannot distinguish between right and wrong, in that they believe that they should have the same share of the good things which their school companions and others enjoy.
The third type, the sexual pervert, develops from some type of maladjustment which cannot be clearly defined and it is a matter that should be referred for proper psychiatric treatment.
When these youngsters, most of whom are simply misguided, appear before a juvenile court judge and the other court officials, they are always, at least in my experience, treated with the greatest consideration. First of all, the law provides that the hearings shall always be secret and in chambers. The youngsters are accompanied by their parents, by their guardians or by other social workers. It is not a court at all in any traditional sense of the word; rather it is simply a heart to heart talk between the judge, who adopts a very fatherly attitude, and the youngster who has diverted from the straight and narrow path. Most of those youngsters appear
Juvenile Delinquents Act before the courts very bewildered and a few questions will soon dissipate the camouflage of self-assurance which they may have and they will generally answer docilely the questions that are put to them by the judge and the judge will truly discover what is the thing that has led them astray. In most instances a few words by the judge, the placing of the youngster on probation for a definite period, either to his own parents, to a court official, or even to a police officer, with definite dates upon which the youngster should report, have the desired effect of changing the youngster's attitude and preventing perhaps the criminal tendencies, which are more or less inherent in all people, from being developed and those youngsters do become very good citizens later on.
I am absolutely in accord with the spirit of the bill presented this afternoon. I approve it, mostly for the same reasons that have been expressed by the previous speaker. There is no doubt at all that even if the greatest precaution is taken to assure that the court records do not fall into hands that should not have them, they will do so and as a matter of fact they often do, and they may be used in much later years, perhaps 10 years or even 20 years later, by unscrupulous blackmailers or other persons against the youngsters who for many years have become respectable citizens of the community.
Even under the present law, although records are secret, although none of the names in the proceedings may be divulged, the record of a juvenile may be used later if that same person, now grown to adulthood, is again before the courts. I believe that is most iniquitous, because surely the youngster when he was a juvenile could not distinguish between right and wrong to the extent that he could do it later when he is no longer in that category and yet, despite that, in certain instances those records are used.
More important perhaps than any other reason is the fact that these records may be destroyed, after five years, as suggested by the bill, gives to the former juvenile a feeling of absolute security and that feeling of security is most necessary to complete his rehabilitation.
For all these reasons I endorse the bill. I believe it is another step forward in the rehabilitation of juveniles and it serves a very useful purpose.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR SECRECY AND DESTRUCTION OF REPORTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on this bill I should simply like to say that one very relevant fact has been brought to my attention, namely that in relation to the population of Canada today there are far too many prison sentences and, in fact, far too many charges

Juvenile Delinquents Act being laid. I say that for one reason. If we compare the population of Canada with that of England we find that in Canada far more people are receiving jail sentences and far more people are being charged, be they juveniles or otherwise.
I should like to go from the general to the particular. I wonder how many hon. members realize how very serious it is for a young person not only to have been charged but sentenced to prison. First of all, when people apply for jobs most companies ask whether they have a record. If they do not ask, then in some unknown way they seem to be able to obtain that information quite easily. I do not know whether I am entirely correct but I make the suggestion that even in many government departments and agencies the question is asked whether the individual has been charged or sentenced to prison. I simply say to the house that most private companies and most government departments and agencies ask this question. But suppose they do not. Here is what usually happens.
I have had a little experience in trying to find work for ex-prisoners. A young fellow may come to your office and say, "Sir, will you help me get a job?". After you have canvassed all the companies that do not ask about a record you may finally get the man a job. But he is then under a serious handicap with respect to whether or not he should inform his employer. Invariably the lad will come to you and say, "Should I inform my employer?". Therefore, irrespective of whether the company has any rules regarding the matter there is always this Damocles sword hanging over his head.
I bring up this matter in order to convey to the house what a very serious proposition we are dealing with. I feel that the records should certainly be destroyed but on the other hand I believe there are certain parts of them that should be retained. I do not mean that part indicating that the person has been charged and sentenced to jail, but that part dealing with the case history of the individual which might have some future relevance and use for psychiatrists. I think such information contained in the records would be useful and as long as the bill guarantees that they will be kept in strict custody I think the bill should receive our approval and support.
In my opinion gross injustice has been done to many young people who have to go through life with this handicap hanging over their heads. For that reason I express my hearty approval and support of the bill. Before taking my seat I wonder whether I might have permission to ask the mover of the bill if it contemplates the destruction of the whole record. Would he inform the

house whether that part of the record that might be of future use for psychiatric purposes in helping the young person would still be retained in proper custody? May 1 put that quesiton to the mover of the bill?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I was interrupted at five o'clock I was relating some of the effects of nuclear bombs and how the effect could be related to the accuracy, as some people have stated. As everyone knows, the effect of the nuclear bomb is related by its co-relation with the effect of one ton of high explosive. When one considers the effect of one ton of high explosive during world

war II, one can roughly gauge the effect of the megaton bomb which is the equivalent of one million tons of high explosive. I want to read to you, Mr. Speaker, and to this house an excerpt from the History of the Second World War, in the volume "Problems of Social Policy", page 329. This is what it says:
In general terms, one ton of high explosives delivered on the built-up areas of London and other large cities destroyed or damaged beyond repair ten houses. Another twenty-five were rendered temporarily uninhabitable, and eighty were slightly damaged. On the average, therefore, one ton affected 115 houses, made eighty people temporarily homeless and caused another thirty-five to lose their homes permanently.
In that event, where then is the need for great accuracy when one considers the effect of the megaton bomb or H-bomb which is the equivalent of one million tons of high explosive? Despite the fact that the prime targets are in the United States, the effect in Canada of short rounds, as the artillery man would say, could be devastating. What then of defence? I am not going to take part in any debate on defence tonight, Mr. Speaker, or of what role our active services or active forces would take in defending us against such a barrage. Let it suffice to say that no matter what the defence, many people will suffer unless we take steps immediately to offset the old-fashioned policy of survival set in operation by the previous administration.
I should like to give to this house and to you, Mr. Speaker, some of the history of civil defence. A planning committee was first set up in Great Britain on May 15, 1924. Its terms of reference were "to inquire into the question of air raid precautions other than naval, military or air defences". Even at that time this committee recommended that while those concerned with maintaining vital services and activities could not be evacuated from important centres such as London, those whose functions were dispensable should be asked and encouraged to leave the target areas. As a result of numerous tests and consultations, the air raid precaution act or, in other words, civil defence act was passed in November, 1937. It imposed on local authorities the duty to take precautions for the protection of persons and property from injury or damage in the event of hostile attack from the air. However, Mr. Speaker, despite the impending catastrophe presaged by Hitler's annexation of Austria, the traditional spirit of local independence vis-a-vis both the central government and other local authorities persisted. It was only after the outbreak of hostilities that great numbers of volunteers came forward to serve in the civil defence. Some 320,000 of these volunteers were paid, but 57071-3-101
The Budget-Mr. Fairfield despite this fact there was all too often dissension among the members as to the role and routine which they were asked to perform.
The Canadian civil defence division is set up under much the same plan as that barely outlined for England. This division was set up in 1948 under the auspices of the Department of National Defence. The terms of reference were to study the requirements of civil defence and make recommendations to the minister as to preparatory and other methods that should be taken to meet a possible emergency. In August, 1950, a dominion-provincial conference was held in Ottawa to determine the division of responsibilities in connection with the building up of a civil defence organization in Canada, and these are the conditions as outlined in that conference.
First of all, the federal government's responsibility was to assess and keep under continuous review the forms and scales of attack to be anticipated in the event of war, and to initiate and guide planning of appropriate civil defence measures; to organize federal services for civil defence; to co-ordinate plans and activities of the provinces and municipalities.
The provincial government was to prepare regional plans and be responsible for preparatory and other measures within their area; to co-ordinate activities of municipalities; to organize provincial services for civil defence.
Third, the municipality's responsibility was for local planning and for organizing municipal services for civil defence; to be responsible for co-ordinating all services and for implementing all civil defence measures in the municipal area.
In February, 1951, the responsibilities relating to civil defence were transferred to the Department of National Health and Welfare. Since that time, much work has been done and many plans have been developed by federal and some provincial and municipal committees, all predicated on the assumption that sufficient warning will be provided by our radar screens.
As I have stated before all this has been changed in the few short months since October of last year. No longer can we depend on warnings of even a few hours. Our warning time has been cut tremendously. Proof is flying around in the skies today that the Russians have ICBM's capable of carrying H-bomb warheads.
The civil defence division has done admirable work under the most difficult conditions of public ennui and sometimes of complete non-participation by local and provincial authorities. A policy has been announced

The Budget-Mr. Fairfield by this government that a fund will be set aside for research into this problem. However, I feel it is imperative that action of a different kind be taken immediately. I cannot impress on this house too strongly that this is no longer a question of civil defence but rather one of civilian survival.
We have at the present time throughout this country a body of men and some women who can, if given the green light, immediately go into action as the optimum means of the survival of our people in the event of a nuclear attack. I speak, of course, of the militia organization in Canada. This organization built around a hard core of veterans, whose survival during the second world war speaks well of their training, I am sure is ready and willing to undertake this task. It is a complicated task, Mr. Speaker. Not only does it require a great deal of training but there is a great basic need of discipline which is too often absent to an alarming degree in groups of civilian volunteers, as was experienced in England during the formative phase of their civilian defence organization.
By granting to the militia the responsibility of this task we would have already shortened the elementary training in discipline, liaison and leadership. Even at the present time 50 per cent of their time is being taken up by civil defence training. I know that there have been protests from some quarters with respect to the militia being relegated to this role but, so far as I know these protests are few indeed. Many militia men have stated to me that they now realize the importance of this training and are prepared to go all out to train their units for duty in the event of disaster. By widespread organization of these units we could bring into the plan those areas which thus far have ignored the appeals of the civil defence division to form active units. Incidentally, the name civil defence in itself does not carry the same weight or meaning as I think it would if it were called home defence.
There have also been objections to having the militia take over civil defence on the grounds that, in the event of war, these units would be mobilized to carry on their normal roles as infantry units, artillery units and so on. In the event of a nuclear attack there will indeed be no time to mobilize units, as the war may well be won or lost in a period of four days.
The wheel has now turned a complete circle. As in the past, the local militia must now be responsible for local survival in the case of a sneak attack. I know that this would require that responsibility for civil defence would have to be assumed by the 

Department of National Defence but this does not indicate any lack of faith in the Department of National Health and Welfare. It would, however, guarantee to a greater degree the co-operation between both active and passive lines of defence. The active training centre for civil defence could carry on the training of militia members. Those who have already been trained in certain aspects of civil defence would be urged to enrol in the militia, thus increasing the capabilities of the organizations which are at present topheavy with officers and senior non-commissioned officers. The militia must realize that this is the role they would be asked to assume and that it is a role which would compare, if not exceed, in importance, at least in the event of nuclear war, those services performed by the active forces.
I would urge the government if such a course is adopted to see that every facility is placed at the disposal of the militia and that its importance with respect to defence should be considered second to none. I realize the expense may be considerable but it would be minor compared with that involved in active defence and would be in no wise comparable to the accruing benefits. The estimated cost of civil defence and of the militia is at the present time in the neighbourhood of $25 million, which is of course a very small part of the total national defence expenditures.
May I repeat that in my opinion passive defence in this day is perhaps even more important than active defence. Certainly from the viewpoint of survival it is of far greater importance. I do not think it would cost this country a great deal more to implement the scheme outlined but even if the costs were doubled-and I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) will not thank me for this suggestion-the need for reorganization and modernization of our civil defence set-up is so great that it can no longer be ignored.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks on the budget. First of all I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), who has at last given us an accounting of our national affairs. His budget speech was longer than that of any previous minister of finance to whom I have listened and my first thoughts were that he would surely end the 1957-1958 budget year with a surplus. He had announced in December and also later in the last session that he would have a surplus and I have in mind the ringing words

of the minister when he was in the opposition, as recorded at page 2555 of Hansard for March 21, 1957:
We wish to see a balanced budget because we believe in a balanced budget.
I felt sure then that the minister would want to complete at least one year in the black. If he had just waited a month or two longer before meddling with the budget of his predecessor he would indeed have had a surplus. Now we have a deficit. Never again do I expect to see the Minister of Finance, or for that matter the Conservative party, come so close to a surplus. You might wonder why I should say that. It is interesting for hon. members to note that only twice since confederation has any Conservative government brought in a surplus budget of as much as $1 million. This government seems to be getting right into step.
I quite agree that we should budget for a deficit if our economy requires it. We should budget for a purpose and we should certainly budget to put our unemployed back to work. However, there is so little design or purpose in this budget that the minister has slipped into a whopping deficit through default and he has been very modest in stating the amount of that deficit. In one two-hour speech the minister was able to reveal to the people of Canada that he would collect and spend all the taxes he could this year plus everything that has been saved over the last decade for a rainy day. In one swoop he has swept us back to our debt structure of 1948. I look with apprehension toward his next budget speech in eight or nine months' time.
I listened to the budget speech finding it hard to associate the words of the minister with the words he used not long ago to the effect that the Canadian people were overtaxed by $500 million, and that each family was overtaxed by $120 per year. He said furthermore that this amount of $120 could be returned to each family and we would still have a balanced budget. I could hardly believe my ears, remembering as I did that the minister had always claimed that the people should always have their own money to spend and that it was their right to have their own money to spend. Yet I heard him state in his budget speech that if it is left with the people it is neither wholly spent nor put into productive investment. The budget indicates to me that the minister will certainly see it is wholly spent.
The minister announced with some finality last fall that the rise in the cost of living had been checked, only to have it reach a new all-time height since that time. We all know that money rates depend largely upon the old law of supply and demand, but 57071-3-10H
The Budget-Mr. McMillan if we follow the minister's own pronouncements we are led to believe that he and he alone loosened up tight money when in fact the demand for money has fallen; even now interest rates on bonds are beginning to tighten up in anticipation of the minister's insatiable desire for new money.
The Minister of Finance was always very critical of his predecessors in office because they were not more accurate in their forecasting. With about three-quarters of the 1957-58 budgetary year already elapsed, the minister estimated a surplus of $80 million, and it turned out that he had a deficit of $39 million-a difference of about $120 million in three months. What might we expect from his prediction for a whole year? Even with the budget he brought in the other night the Minister of Finance had an advantage over his predecessors to the extent that the budget year 1958-59 was already under way. His real test will come in budget No. 2, presented we hope before the next financial year begins on April 1, 1959.
The Minister of Finance should be adept at mathematics. I suggest that if he knows anything about addition and subtraction he was misled by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who last year refused to face the facts of life in connection with mathematics. The Prime Minister travelled from coast to coast telling the people of Canada they were over-taxed by $500 million, that each family was over-taxed by $120 and that the government was reaching into the pockets of each man, woman and child and taking out $30. speechtext:
I am not going to say that I did not refer to my notes occasionally, but I would add this: that the figures in the budget are so illogical that you have to refer to notes or you will never get anywhere.
Now, I said a while ago that our economy is sick, and that the Minister of Finance does not think it is sick because the other night he said, after all, this is a fairly mild recession. I think you will find those words in his budgetary speech. I suggest that the minister has given our economy a placebo pill when more vigorous treatment would have been desirable. I understand that if Mr. Harris' budget had been carried through until March 31 we would have had a surplus. It looks as though this government is costing the people a billion dollars in the first fiscal year, not counting the million lost to this country through unemployment. It is true that money rates have fallen since they got into power, but these lower rates were not given to the people buying homes. They were not given the advantage of these lower rates. I say that when the government's demand for money hits the market, the rates will rise.
The gross national product was $31.4 billion last year, an increase of 4 per cent over that of 1956. The minister is basing his revenue on $32 billion this year, a 2 per cent increase. I have heard and read accounts to the effect that the minister is taking too high a base. I hope that he is low and that our gross national product is more. However, from observations, and from seeing the number of people who are being added to the rolls of the unemployed, I would doubt this very much. I think this figure might well be high. I have no doubt the minister put forth the most optimistic figure he could obtain. The government will not make any confidential reports available to the members of the house, on anything. Even if we accept the $32 billion as the minister's base, he is admitting a bad year because we need an expanding economy to take up the number of new people coming in to the labour market. The increase last year was 4 per cent, but we still had a large number of unemployed.
I should like to ask the minister if he does not expect the number of unemployed will be greatly increased because we are only having a 2 per cent increase this year in the gross national product. I will admit that here I shall have to refer to notes a little bit in order to quote these figures accurately. The minister admits his budgetary expenditures for the year ending next March 31 will be $5,300 million, up $215 million, and

his income will be $4,660 million, down $387 million. He will have a budgetary deficit of $640 million. I was interested in the financial acrobatics utilized by the Minister of Finance to grab off $165 million from the defence equipment account in order to avoid showing a deficit of $800 million or more.
I understand that this money is just a set of figures in the government books. The amount is one of the non-budgetary accounts and will now be transferred to the budgetary account. The fact is that this money does not exist. By liquidating this account the minister spends $165 million in the budgetary accounts and borrows it from the Canadian people as money for capital account. This is like the merchant who made money last year, but lost money this year. In order to make up his losses this year, he goes to his profits of last year, but he is down. This $165 million has to be borrowed before we can use it. It is not there now. This is somewhat like a little game of pretence. A man might owe $100, but he has no money. He used to have a bank account, but there is nothing in it and there is nothing in his pocket. He is pressed for this $100, so he writes a cheque for the $100. Then, he rushes around and borrows $100 from some one which he puts in the bank before the cheque is presented. Certainly, he has paid, one account, but he still owes $100. However, that is Conservative financing.
The point is that the Canadian taxpayer will owe an extra $165 million which was not debt before, no matter whether you call it a budgetary or non-budgetary account. We get returns from most of these non-budgetary accounts such as those in crown corporations and the St. Lawrence seaway. This money will eventually be paid back, but the $165 million is just going to be heavy debt. There are other amounts to be included in this year's expenses, such as the final supplementary estimates and further statutory expenditures on which the minister does not show a very bright light. Then, there are the final payments to the provinces, and the minister himself said that those already made were only interim payments.
On page 1240 of Hansard the minister says that the house has before it the estimates and supplementary estimates amounting to $5,237 million. According to his own figures we will be paying out close to $70 million under the provisions of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, plus $190 million for increased deficits in the old age security fund, plus a Canadian National deficit of at least $55 million, bringing the total expenditure to $5,552 million. It is at this point that the minister neatly subtracts
The Budget-Mr. McMillan $165 million from the national defence equipment account, bringing the amount down to $5,387 million, and calling it approximately $5,300 million-the $87 million does not amount to much. I maintain he had no right to do this.
If we take this $5,552 million, before this subtraction is made, we have yet to include in our expenditures for the year the increases to the civil service, the increased payments to the provinces and the further supplementary estimates. As the minister states in the budget, his estimate of income is $4,660 million. This only allows him $108 million for those three and other items, after which his deficit is $1 billion. To all intents and purposes, this is a billion dollar deficit budget, and I will not be surprised if it is well over this amount. The minister's baby budget turned out one year later to be a deficit. This baby is a billion dollar bouncing deficit. "Bouncing" is probably the wrong word because it is a dead weight.
The minister is very obscure about the figures in his non-budgetary operating accounts. For instance, he states that other non-budgetary costs and requirements, including the liquidation of the defence equipment account, will be of the order of $240 million. We know that the defence equipment account amounts to $165 million, so what of the other $75 million? Is $75 million so small an amount that the minister does not feel it is worth mentioning? What is it for? I heard the minister talk much about "What's a million?" I would like to ask him what is $75 million? What is it for?
After looking at all the figures one finds that the Minister of Finance depleted the cash account by $163 million last year, and he will be going to the people for $1,400 million of new money. This is the amount of money the government must borrow and this amount will be added to our public debt. This is equivalent to a debt of $80 for every man, woman and child in Canada. This amount is equal to a debt of $325 per family of four, and to this we must add the interest over the years.
I was interested in one of the government accounts, namely account No. 33, which shows a depletion of $131 million in the unemployment insurance account. I know this amount has nothing whatever to do with the budget, but it shows how the government has succeeded also in getting this account into an actuarial mess.
The minister always complained about the waste and extravagance of former governments. I remember him saying that we had too many civil servants, and he could have been right. But, according to the blue book, I notice-and I have added up the figures in

that in his own department, and in his own department alone, the minister has 70 more civil servants working tor him than his predecessor had last year.

speechtext:
It is rather interesting to examine a table entitled "Summary of Standard Objects of Special Expenditure and Special Categories". It is contained in a separate sheet attached to the back of the estimates book this year. Without, of course, including the supplementary estimates, the table gives the proposed expenditures of each department of government under 22 "standard objects" and "special categories". This classification makes it possible to compare and to see how the expenditures change in the different departments from year to year. Under objects 1, 2, 3 and 21, which include civil salaries and wages, civil allowances, pay and allowances, defence forces and R.C.M.P. pensions, superannuation and other benefits, we find the estimates up $108 million. This increase seems general to all departments. Item No. 4, professional and special services is up $10.2 million, but items 5 and


12 show an over-all decrease because of the reduction of expenditures in national defence; but the totals of all these items for the other departments have increased.
When we come to item 13, under the heading "Building and works, including construction and acquisition", it is here that we find all works of a capital nature to be paid out of the budgetary estimates. These latter estimates are increased from only $358.7 million last year to $380.3 million this year, an increase of $21.6 million. This seems a small increase, particularly this year, having in mind the Prime Minister's promised works program of $1,185 million for unemployment. Included in this amount-that is the increase of $21.6 million-is an increase of $8.1 million for Northern Affairs and National Resources, which is hardly in keeping with a great northern vision.
The minister lays considerable stress on the increased payments under the welfare measures initiated by the former government. Desirable as these payments are-and I agree with them-they are not productive of wealth. We must get our unemployed back to work and get them producing. They would prefer work to unemployment insurance benefits that are now running out.
This government seems to have an idea that it can spend the country out of a recession. This cannot be done without providing work for our people. This government seems to have the mental complex of a man who came to my office some time ago. He had an issue of the Toronto Globe and Mail in his pocket which carried an article on the amount of liquor that had been sold in Ontario in the previous year. It went on to tell how much had accrued to the coffers of the Ontario government through the sale of this liquor. I know the sum was considerable; I have forgotten the exact amount. This man made rather a peculiar observation. He said, "I believe we will drink ourselves out of debt yet". This is much the same type of reasoning this government uses in thinking it can spend the country out of this recession when so many of our people are unemployed and not engaged in productive industry. I feel sorry for these people. They have commitments to meet; they have payments to meet. They want to own and live in comfortable homes and Canada owes them more than just a mere living. They have hopes and aspirations as the rest of us have, and they should work and be able to have a standard of living commensurate with that of their fellow Canadians.
Let the government get back to the idea of expanding trade instead of diverting it. When the buying commission went to Britain we had much unemployment in this country while employment was fairly good in Britain.

The first order was a good-will order by the Ontario hydro consisting of some millions of dollars for the purchase of generator equipment. I was told in the house that generators were being ordered by the Ontario hydro which had never been made in Canada in that particular size; they were very large. I found out afterwards this was true but I also found out that they had never before been made in England.
I know of one industry at least in the Niagara district which was figuring on supplying some component parts of these generators. If that order had been placed in Canada there would certainly not be so many electrical workers unemployed in the Toronto, Hamilton, Niagara and Peterborough districts.
During the election campaign the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) was in Port Colborne and at that time he said that the government was going to divert more trade. Up to that time they had diverted quite a lot of trade, and I think the people of my constituency elected me because they did not want to see a lot more trade diverted. I am afraid that our government in its zeal to divert trade has taken jobs from Canadians in that British manufactured goods are coming into Canada more and more to compete with the output of our own industries.
Following the start of the trans-Canada pipe line the Welland Tubes plant was built at a cost of many millions of dollars to make large diameter pipe for trans-Canada and other companies. I would hope that the government would insist on all-Canadian pipe since the government is guaranteeing part of the cost of the trans-Canada line through northern Ontario.
Some of the unemployed in my area voted for the government because the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) said that unemployment would be cleared up by summer. Summer has arrived and this coming week we will have 500 more unemployed in Welland. I appeal to the government to help the unemployed get back to work. I agree with Premier Bennett of British Columbia who is reported as having said in the legislature on March 7 that it is time for the federal government to quit playing politics and to get down to the business of government.
Surely time is running out when the government can continue to blame unemployment on the former government. Never in the history of a Liberal government have we ever had so many unemployed in any corresponding month as we have had this year under the present government. Surely it is time to give more thought to a budget
The Budget-Mr. T. M. Bell than just to raise the cost of government in each department without doing something at the same time to provide work for the unemployed. I should like to see the Minister of Finance use his own imagination in drawing up a budget rather than to follow the dictates of the Prime Minister. It seems to me that he is enough of a financial wizard to do some adding and subtracting and not present us with such a deficit.
I regret that there is nothing new in the budget for higher education. I thought the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) was probably giving a lead to the Conservative government when he promised students in Vancouver that there would be more money for higher education. I admire the minister's ability as an educator and I agree with his statement as reported in the press that we as a free western nation should make a concerted effort to help technological education. The Minister of Finance is just making a pretence of helping higher education by granting corporations a ten per cent exemption for educational donations instead of five per cent of their net profits. Contributions thus far have only been a fraction of the five per cent. How does the minister expect to get more by raising the exemption to ten per cent?

speechtext: Order. It is with regret that I interrupt the hon. member but I must inform him that his time has expired.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I can remember that all the clocks in the chamber have stopped at the same time. I do not suggest any particular reason why it has happened but it may be that it is creating additional difficulty in the timing of speeches. This is the first major debate for some time in which I have taken part. I want to extend congratulations to the new members who have spoken so nobly. With the great talents that many of them have, it is easy to see why the rest of us are beginning to fade away.
But I have also risen to take part in the debate because in recent years it has become traditional for maritime members to put on record some of the economic facts of life of the maritimes during the budget address. The other evening the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) went back into history to 1911 and 1930 for comparisons with the present budget and our economic situation. I went back a little bit farther, Mr. Speaker, to 1867. This came to my mind when I was reviewing the history of a distinguished gentleman who many years ago represented the constituency I now represent and who in the first parliament was

The Budget-Mr. T. M. Bell minister of customs and in the second parliament minister of finance. One could not help but note the comparison of economic conditions at that time and those that exist today although I admit there are similarities in the case of the other two years I have just mentioned. One thinks that at that time there was the national policy of Sir John A. Macdonald and today we have the new nationbuilding, national development policy of the present Conservative government. At that time there was a railway to be built to the west. Today it is roads to the north. There is a similarity also in that at that time and also today young men and a new government were involved. There was an expanding economy and there was need for reasonable protection.
We all realize the dangers of tariffs. They are something like the sailor's tattoo. They are easy to put on but hard to get off. But I think it is within traditional Conservative policy to have some reasonable protection. Of course, the question may be asked: What were the Liberals doing during this postconfederation period and what are they doing today? speechtext:
There are 56,000 unemployed in the Atlantic Provinces. I know it is a little disheartening for the Liberal party not to be able to have these high figures about which to make their gloomy speeches.
However, I would like to turn to the second disability suffered by the Atlantic provinces ever since confederation. I hope to make some constructive suggestions which might be considered in order to improve the future for the area.
Secondly, there is the problem of transportation. We had a meeting of the maritimes transportation commission in Saint John about two weeks ago and the officials of the commission said in their report that matters showed some improvement but that we need continuing vigilance due to the changing state of the transportation system, not only in the Atlantic provinces but in the whole of Canada. Transportation everywhere in this country is in a state of flux; it is in a state of transformation and in the Atlantic area particularly we have to watch every movement of transportation.
First of all with respect to road transportation I do hope that the government in their roads program will be able to find some formula to enable improvements to be carried out in the Atlantic provinces. It may be that a method can be found to make these improvements by means of tourist access roads or it may be that roads for the development of our resources can be combined with roads for the tourist industry. The tourist industry is, of course, extremely important and I can think in my own constituency of a very


definite need for a road along the coast at the bay of Fundy. We have no trail such as the Cabot trail in Nova Scotia or the Gaspe trail in Quebec. There is certainly room for a lovely Fundy trail to enable us to build up the tourist industry which means so much to us in terms of dollars. Such an undertaking is a tremendous one for a provincial government but perhaps a formula could be worked out jointly between the federal or provincial authorities. Similarly the resource development programs could be assisted by the means of new roads helping to balance out the economy of our country.
Secondly, with respect to water transportation we have been watching the movements of the St. Lawrence area, not only so far as tolls are concerned but also with respect to continued efforts to keep the seaway open further down the St. Lawrence each year. We feel that we may have to give our trade and export business during the winter months a new look. This St. Lawrence seaway program appears to be a very prosperous undertaking and perhaps it will be possible to include the development of the Chignecto canal in conjunction with the seaway, thereby further balancing out our problems as the seaway expands and as the economy of this country is concentrated further inland and our transportation disparities increase.
Thirdly, there is the matter of air transportation. In the maritimes we have a climate which creates more problems than that in many sections of this country and therefore our air transportation undoubtedly takes on a new importance. It may be that more competition is necessary with respect to air transportation in our area, even though revenues would not at first glance be so great.
Fourthly, and perhaps most important is the problem of rail transportation which is still very serious in our area. A nation as great as ours must, of course, always face great difficulties in this respect. In 1926 we received the benefit of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. These benefits have, of course, assisted us to some extent but the horizontal increases since this time have tended to cut down that assistance and today the agreed charges which at the time seemed fair have, in fact, worked out against our interest because our manufacturers are not large enough and cannot take sufficient advantage of them. I think we have only about 30 agreed charges out of the 400 which are in effect.
I have attempted to point out the disabilities under which we are living with respect to power and transportation. While we feel that a good start has been made with respect to the problem of power, our problems with respect to transportation still have

a long way to go. The hon. member lor Gloucester made the suggestion the other day that perhaps an agency should be set up as a continuing body to look after our transportation problems. While I am not sure that in these changing days a continuing agency is necessary I do feel his suggestion has a lot of merit. We must watch the movements which are taking place in a modern world, but we have an optimistic approach to the future and look forward to taking our proper place in the economy of Canada.
Someone has said, very unkindly, that as far as the maritimes are concerned, the smart fellows moved out west, and the smarter they were the quicker they moved. We who have stayed in the maritimes, however, believe that the smart guys left because they could not stand the competition. As far as we are concerned it is a fine budget and we in the maritimes look forward to a continuing development under the new administration.
