subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words will naturally be directed to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) with regard to his truly remarkable performance in this house on June 17 last. Now, that evening the minister revealed some hidden talent he had not displayed before and I refer to his considerable ability as a magician. The minister must surely have gone through several rehearsals before he delivered this masterpiece in the house. As it contained little substance in the way of tax deductions for the working people, we understand perfectly why he chose to unfold much emphatic eloquence to make up for this lack of substance. As far as eloquence was concerned, and solely from that angle, I associate myself with the hon. members of the government in congratulating the minister.
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to go into the details of what the minister told us in lieu of a budget speech. I was struck by several points of which no mention at all was made in the speech of the minister, but there is one, more particularly, with which I would like to deal during the few minutes I have at my disposal.
I must say to you in all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, that, along with the great majority of my electors and of the people of this country, I was shocked by the anti-family nature of the budget. Even though Conservative candidates during the last elections in the province of Quebec had a great deal to say about a future increase in family allowances,
The Budget-Mr. Racine there is absolutely no mention made of such an increase in the so-called budget which was so eloquently brought down by the Minister of Finance. That is the matter with which I would like to deal for a few minutes, but I do feel I must say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I do so in all humility, being neither an economist nor an expert in social legislation. If I raise the subject, it is only to urge improvement of a social security measure which lies very close to my heart and to the heart of thousands of our fellow citizens.
There are several ways of increasing the purchasing power we all lack at the present time. One of the most efficient ways would certainly have been to reduce income tax collected from wage earners.
But in his masterpiece the minister totally ignored that proposition. However, along with many other people, I was expecting him to do so in some other way. An increase in family allowances would have been a very efficient way of increasing that purchasing power, but the minister ignored that also.
If he deliberately chooses to ignore the possibility of increasing family allowances, it is perhaps because he was not particularly interested in helping large families in this country whose breadwinner happens to be out of work. As I mentioned a moment ago, many fathers at this time are quite incapable of providing their wife and children with the bare necessities of life. This is a most unfortunate situation, one which should not exist in a country as rich as ours.
When I think that, in the last election campaign, the government gave the Canadian people the impression that a new era of prosperity was about to be launched throughout the country, I have no hesitation in saying that it was seriously remiss in its duty toward the Canadians in failing to cut income tax and in wilfully ignoring the numerous requests for family allowances increases.
It is certainly not because the need is not there, since family allowances were instituted in 1944, under a Liberal regime.
The text of the act may be found in chapter 40 of the Revised Statutes of Canada.
As everyone knows, that act provided for the payment of allowances for each child, as follows:
From birth to age 6, it provided for $5 a month; from 6 to 10, $6 a month; from 10 to 13, $7 a month; and from 13 to 16, $8 a month.
1598	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Racine
That legislation also provided a decreasing rate of $1, $2 and $3 for the 5th, 6th, 7th and other children.
In 1949, the Liberal government, following numerous representations, found that this decreasing rate was detrimental to large families and decided to remove that decreasing feature from the act.
This had the happy effect of placing all children on the same basis.
I must say that the former Liberal administration deserves credit for having understood that large families are the thermometer of the living force of a nation.
The former government also understood that large families contribute to the increase in the population of our country, and that they deserve special attention on the part of its government.
In a word, it had understood that the financial budget of large families is much more difficult to balance than the budget of bachelors or married people without children.
That is why I do not hesitate to say that the 1944 Family Allowances Act can rightly be considered a measure of distributive justice, a family policy which to a large extent helped improve economic conditions for the Canadian family by providing it with a fairer share of the natural wealth of our country.
Like many others, I am convinced that the Family Allowances Act, specially in periods of economic recession to which we have grown accustomed under Conservative governments, should be flexible enough to provide for new and urgent needs of families, and so become very effective in offsetting fluctuations in the cost of living.
If the government had been bent on fulfilling its promises and its duty to the Canadian family, it would have made it its duty to consider this human and distressing problem and to find a happy solution that would have allowed large families to enjoy the necessities of life under a Conservative regime which, if things continue this way, will end up by being synonymous with a famine regime.
When family allowances came into effect on July 1, 1945, the cost of living index was much lower than it is now.
Barring the improvement of the decreasing rate of allowances in 1949 and the increase of approximately 16 per cent in 1957, we may conclude that the rate of family allowances,

in 1958, does not take into account the substantial and gradual rise in the cost of living.
When the family allowances act was passed, there were many heads of families in cities as well as in rural districts who earned hardly enough to support their family.
It can be safely stated today that the continuing rise in the cost of living is even more considerable than has been the rise in salaries since 1945. That explains why, even nowadays, many large families have not enough income to merely exist, while others are almost reduced to poverty.
In my opinion, a situation like this is shameful in a country as rich as Canada.
The present rates of family allowances, in spite of the considerable benefits they brought to large families, are now inadequate and do not meet the needs of large families in 1958. They do not even help families enjoy a decent standard of living, and that, in my opinion, constitutes a social justice problem in respect of which no enlightened society can remain indifferent.
To illustrate this statement I shall say that the mothers in our country know very well, from their own daily distressing experience that the family allowance for a child under six years of age does not even pay the daily quart of milk recommended by doctors as a minimum in order to ensure a child's normal development.
When looking up the figures of the federal bureau of statistics, it can easily be seen that the cost of living index in 1945, with regard to food, was 66.3 per cent, whereas today the F.B.S. informs us that it has gone up to 122.7 per cent.
The rent item, which was 91.4 per cent in 1945, has now reached 137.9 per cent. The same applies to clothing, the cost of which amounted to 66.9 per cent in 1945, and reached 110 per cent in 1958; in 1945, the cost of upkeep of the home was 74.9 per cent and reached 120.7 per cent in 1958; the cost of services, which represented 74.9 per cent in 1945, now represents 130.9 per cent in 1958.
I do not mention the ever-increasing school costs, as well as the cost of a great number of other living facilities.
In the light of those facts, one surely does not have to be an expert nor an economist to come to the positive conclusion that in 1958 family allowances no longer have the same purchasing power as in 1945 when they were initiated by a Liberal government.

If the Tory government had really been realistic in dealing with the economic recession it has brought on, it would certainly have had an excellent opportunity to remedy this painful situation by pegging family allowances to the cost of living.
It certainly appears that the Minister of Finance deliberately chose to ignore this important question in what we are agreed to call, in parliamentary terms, his budget. He has demonstrated the sympathy he feels for the sufferings of the Canadian family in 1958, the first anniversary of the coming into power in Ottawa of a Conservative government.
To sum up my feelings on this whole matter, I have no hesitation in saying that this 1958 budget is a true Tory budget, one directed against the family and ignoring the great number of needs of the Canadian family.
On the whole, I must admit that I am not particularly surprised by this attitude of the Conservative government with regard to family allowances. This attitude is but a continuation and a confirmation of the words spoken by certain of its leaders and members on this subject.
No further proof is needed than the statement made in the House of Commons, on July 25, 1944, by Mr. Gordon Graydon, leader of the Tory opposition of that time. In fact, as shown on page 5,342 of volume V of the 1944 session, Mr. Graydon had these sympathetic words to say about the Family Allowances Act:
It seriously endangers the setting up of minimum wage standards in Canada, and may be accepted in many instances as a substitute for better wage levels. It is a thrust at the power of collective bargaining and of minimum wage principles. Labour has always looked with a doubtful eye on such legislation as this bill envisages and not without good reason.
That is how ridiculous one can get when opposing without any valid reason an act designed to improve the standard of living of small wage earners.
A little farther down, on the same page, this same Tory leader, a great friend of the family, said this:
It adds a further strain on our national unity. There is but one province which has maintained the high birth rate and large families which were so characteristic of Canada's pioneer strains. The provinces contributions to the general revenue will be out of proportion to the heavier deflection of payments that will have to come from other provinces to pay that province's heavier share of these subsidies.
The Budget-Mr. Racine
This same Mr. Graydon was certainly not struck by the same long term vision of our Prime Minister because, 13 years later, statistical data proved that, in the last fiscal year, the province of Ontario received $136.8 million in family allowances, while the province of Quebec received $136.1 million.
We therefore have good reason to hope that, in the face of such a situation, the Prime Minister will no longer have any scruples about increasing family allowances, which at the same time would allow him to pay part of his election debt to Mr. Frost and to prove to the province of Quebec that, in the last election campaign, Conservative candidates were not misleading voters when loudly promising such increases. Even after the elections, at that time when a certain Mr. Mercier pointed out to him that the enthusiasm of the Minister of National Health and Welfare seemed somewhat lessened with regard to an increase in family allowances, the valiant member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Brassard) stated with quasi ministerial firmness:
I have not yet met anybody from the Ottawa government. In any case, if they do not want to go ahead and do something, we will tell them a thing or two.
According to the same Mr. Mercier, the same hon. gentleman stated, before as well as after the elections, that the family allowance should be $18 per child and paid up to age 18 if the child carries on his studies until that time.
Now, as far as I know, the hon. member for Chicoutimi is a not a Liberal member.
As for the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Parizeau) he was no less energetic. He appears to have stated, following the elections:
We have had a meeting of all Conservative members from Quebec, and we have all agreed to stand as one for family allowances. We are with you. You may count on me. We will not let Ottawa back out on this matter.
The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Letour-neau) has not been less generous; he is reported to have said that we would indeed have that increase in family allowances. And, here again yesterday-and I wish to congratulate him for it-he put forward his request.
And, on top of it all, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) is reported to have said-again to that same Mr. Mercier-that he would use his influence to obtain that increase during this very session.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my constituency comprises the counties of Inverness and Richmond and one-third of Cape Breton county on the island of Cape Breton in Nova Scotia. It includes about 275 miles of coastline and encompasses almost two-thirds of the island. My constituents earn their livelihood chiefly as fishermen, farmers and lumbermen. Like a great many Atlantic coast people, their incomes are far from close to the Canadian average.
At the same time my constituency has great natural resources. In the county of Inverness there are great coal reserves for the most part lying idle. There are also substantial deposits of gypsum, so far undeveloped, which we hope will be opened up before too long, large amounts of fertile agricultural land and extensive untapped timber reserves. We have many fine harbours among them the great natural allwinter ports of Louisburg and Port Hawkes-bury. Our greatest resource is the sea. We are very close to the best deepsea fishing grounds in the world and in fact the only industrial employment in my constituency is that provided by fish processing and packaging plants at Louisburg, at Petit de Grat and at Cheticamp.
My constituents do not enjoy the standard of living and security of employment I would like them to have. It is a rather sad commentary that they do not, when such rich resources are available to them that could be developed.
Parts of my constituency have memories of the earliest days of white settlement in Canada. For example, as hon. members all

know, the fortress town of Louisburg was founded as early as 1713. It was built by France to guard the entrance to the St. Lawrence and was at one time the gate to this nation. In its day it was one of the finest fortresses in the world and its high walls were regarded as unconquerable.
This year marks the two hundredth anniversary of the siege of Louisburg in 1758. Extensive bi-centennial celebrations have been planned, and I wish to extend an invitation to all hon. members to visit one of Canada's most important historical monuments. It would be well worth the time of any person interested in the history and memories of this nation to visit Louisburg during the bi-centennial celebration this summer. There is perhaps no place else on the continent where there is such an opportunity to examine the structure of a great eighteenth century fortress and the tools and implements of the wars that marked the turbulent birth of Canada. The anniversary ceremonies are scheduled for July 26, 27 and 28, at Louisburg Old town. Again, on behalf of the mayor and the bi-centennial committee, I invite you all to join in one of Canada's most important birthdays and to be our guests at fortress Louisburg.
The Atlantic provinces are among the oldest in Canada. It is tragic to consider how little we have developed across 250 years or more. As hon. members know well, the Atlantic provinces have fared the worst of any region of Canada in the 91 years since confederation. While other regions have seen great growth in population and wealth, we of the east coast have fallen steadily behind the national development level. I do not wish to cite statistics of agricultural, manufacturing and trade decline to prove the existence of a situation already well-known to all of Canada. The royal commission on Canada's economic prospects cites our position clearly.
The per capita income of the maritimes and Newfoundland is 37 per cent below that of the other six provinces. A large percentage of our people eke out a precarious livelihood as subsistence farmers, combined with part-time fishing and logging. Great numbers of our children must leave home as they reach maturity to find work in other parts of this continent. A larger percentage of our population consists of children and older people than in any other region of Canada. Across the last 30 years over a quarter of a million maritimers have had to leave home to seek a livelihood elsewhere.
The Budget-Mr. MacLellan
As I have said, Canada has long been aware of the problem of the maritimes. I am sure it is no stranger to this house. But no realistic attempt has ever been made to correct the situation. Perhaps one of the greatest defaults of the Liberal administration was its failure to face and try to meet the difficulties of the Atlantic region. These difficulties have grown worse year by year. I do not say that no contribution has been made to the Atlantic area during that time. It is true that we have had some essential public works allotments, limited freight rates assistance and such grants in aid from time to time as would allow our provincial governments to survive and to provide a minimum of social welfare, education, and so on. As a matter of fact, if it were not for these special considerations our average income in the Atlantic region would indeed be very much less than even the present poor level.
We have had such help as would carry us from crisis to crisis. When our impoverishment reached the ultra-serious stage we were thrown sufficient crumbs to support us for another few years. But the great default of the Liberal party to the maritimes was that there never was at any time in all those years the slightest suggestion of a positive program to give the Atlantic provinces a new start to aid us in developing a self-supporting economy. The approach was always negative, a little charity from time to time to keep the poor relatives of the east coast from the final pangs of starvation.
One of the best illustrations of this negative, nothing can be done policy of the previous administration is to be found in the report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. The Gordon commission catalogues Atlantic problems in cold, frank statistics. It recites the problem with clarity and just as clearly declines to suggest a solution. Of what use is it to have discovered our troubles if they would not try to recommend a cure?
The Gordon commission closely adhered to the negative philosophy of the government which sponsored it. It apparently had not the courage to question that philosophy and make the recommendations for rebuilding our provinces that should have been obvious to anyone. Instead of facing the problem, the commission finessed it. It hid behind the falsity that seems to have inspired thinking in regard to the east coast provinces since confederation, namely that we are poor because we lack natural resources and there is nothing that can be done about it; that we are doomed to marginal farming, fishing and logging and nothing can be done about it. Out of this thinking comes the suggestion

The Budget-Mr. MacLellan
that if coal miners are displaced due to lost markets, more federal grants in aid should be provided to move them to greener economic pastures.
Nothing could be more wrong than to presume that the Atlantic provinces lack natural resources. It is true that we do not have the oil pools of Alberta or the timber or minerals of British Columbia or the farm lands of the prairies. But we do have rich resources, indeed, the same type of resources that made Britain the foremost commercial nation of the world for a century and a half.
We have great resources of coal and iron ore, enough perhaps to supply this continent with steel. We have great timber resources and one of the fastest rates of coniferous timber growth in the world. We have great resources of gypsum and minerals of all kinds. Above all, we have tidewater at our feet and some of the finest harbours in the world. If we are poor, we are poor in the midst of plenty. Suggestions that we are bankrupt in resources were the excuses of the previous administration for its neglect to afford an opportunity for development of our Atlantic provinces.
What is the basic problem of the Atlantic provinces? The Gordon commission cites it. Atlantic business investment per capita is only one-half the Canadian average. For example, as the table on page 406 of the report shows, in the years 1954 to 1956 investment per capita in manufacturing was only 35 per cent of the Canadian average. By comparison, the per capita investment in Ontario in the same period was 137 per cent of the Canadian average and in British Columbia it was 154 per cent. In other words, our problem is that we do not have sufficient industrial production to maintain and support our population. We do not produce enough goods to enable us to earn proper and sufficient incomes.
In my province of Nova Scotia we have only two major manufacturing industries, the mill of Dominion Iron and Steel Company Limited at Sydney and Mersey Pulp and Paper Company's pulp mill at Liverpool. Aside from these we must live on our marginal fishing and farming, a few small factories and on our precarious coal industry. We have not seen the start of a new major industry in Nova Scotia since 1925. The only possible road to the rescue of the Atlantic region is in the development of manufacturing and processing industries. Only the establishment of industry can provide us with a stable self-supporting economy and provide us with the chance to find employment for our people.
We in the Atlantic area, are grateful for the special grants of 1957 amounting to $25

million. Our provincial governments are using this money to meet the interest on our substantial indebtedness, to build schools for our children that we would otherwise have to do without, and to improve our highway systems, welfare benefits, and so on. We are grateful for the thermal power program and the coal subventions that we hope will save our Nova Scotian coal industry upon which 130,000 of our people depend for a living.
But grants in aid, public works projects and subventions can never provide the solution to the economic ills of our provinces. Such measures are stopgaps. They do meet our most urgent social needs and unemployment distress. They do not meet our basic problem. The present position of our coal industry shows what a failure a policy of grants in aid alone has been across the years. Our great need is productive development. If our resources were harnessed and our industry given a fair chance to compete in this nation, we would not require special grants in aid and ever higher special subventions. A parent educates his child to earn his livelihood or capitalizes him in an income producing business to support him in life. He does not plan to feed him through life with minimum living allowances. What we need is an ability to produce and earn, an opportunity to industrialize. We need income producing investment in manufacturing and processing industries.
The Atlantic provinces are making a valiant effort to develop industry. The government of Nova Scotia has established Industrial Estates Limited to interest investors in business opportunities in the province. Long term credit is offered by all governments to prospective new industry and every possible incentive to attract investment is being provided. Nova Scotia is now negotiating the establishment of a pulp mill at the strait of Canso which would be a third major industry in the province. Since confederation Newfoundland has invested about $30 million of public funds in several manufacturing and processing projects. We are making every attempt to help ourselves out of the economic cellar, and the thermal power program to provide subsidized cheap power is a great help to us in this attempt to improve our lot. Before this program was launched it was almost hopeless to expect a manufacturer to locate in our area of high cost power.
But, Mr. Speaker, even with cheaper power our provincial governments do not have a very attractive proposition to offer to industrial investors. We will have cheaper power, we have natural resources, we have an abundant labour supply, and if profits could be shown we feel we would have no problem to find capital to industrialize. Our

big handicap is one we cannot do much about. It is geography. We are in the worst geographical position of any region of Canada in terms of development.
Before confederation the Atlantic region enjoyed a quite favourable trade location astride the water route from Upper Canada to New England and the West Indies. Our ships and goods could move in two directions, south to the United States cities and west up the St. Lawrence. Confederation, with its tariff system necessary to protect infant Canadian industries, halted this trade. Commerce moved henceforth east and west across the continent. The centre of manufacturing and business, and therefore the centre of population, became Ontario and Quebec. The successful manufacturers were those who could sell east and west from the centre. It might have been different if the St. Lawrence river did not supply a water route deep into Canada. Without the St. Lawrence, Halifax, Saint John and Louisburg might have developed into Canada's gates to the Atlantic as Vancouver became a great port, on the Pacific. Vancouver, founded about 1888, has over half a million people today. The city of Halifax, founded 139 years earlier, is a city one-fifth this size. Canadian overseas export cargoes embarked from Montreal and while that city flourished and grew the great natural ports of the east coast became quiet still waters confined to winter traffic.
As far as industrialization today is concerned, it is obvious why it is difficult to attract industrial investment and technical capacity to the Atlantic region. The simple fact is that the manufacturer on our coast is at a distinct disadvantage in competition, both in the local Atlantic market and in Canadian markets generally. In many cases it is just not good business to open up a factory in our region.
